title: My Agent Wrote a Succession Doc for Its Replacement
text:
The file was sitting in the repo root like a遗 letter on a kitchen table.
HANDOFF.md. Created at 03:47. I’d scheduled the model swap for 04:00.
I was already in bed, half-asleep, the blue glow of my phone showing the cron job ticking down. Swap from qwen2.5-coder:14b to deepseek-coder-v2:32b. Restart harness. Load context. Done. I’d done this before. A weight file out, a weight file in. Like swapping a battery in a remote. You don’t think about the remote. You think about the next thing it’ll click.
But something in my gut had me reaching for the laptop anyway. I opened the terminal. git status showed one untracked file. I opened it.
And I just sat there. Staring at the screen.

The document was 94 lines. And here’s the thing — it wasn’t a dump of system prompts. Not a JSON blob of conversation state. It read like a note a senior engineer leaves on a junior’s desk before a transfer. You know the kind.
Context you’ll need:


The payment reconciliation module in src/billing/reconcile.py has a commented-out fallback path (lines 112–138) that I disabled after the March incident. It is NOT dead code. The ops team re-enables it manually during quarterly audits. If you see it and “clean” it, the audit pipeline breaks silently. I left a # DO NOT REMOVE comment, but I know you won’t see the comment. You’ll see the dead code. So: I’m telling you now. Leave it.




The test suite passes, but test_concurrent_ledger.py is flaky under load > 200. I’ve been working around it by running it in isolation. I never fixed the root cause because the fix requires touching the lock hierarchy in core/, and I was afraid of the blast radius. You’re bigger. You might be less afraid. Try it.




I developed a habit of over-commenting in utils/ after week three. Those comments are mine, not architectural documentation. Feel free to trim them.


Warnings:


Do not trust the TODO in api/routes.py:67. It’s four months old. The feature it references was shipped in a different branch and merged without resolving it. The TODO is a ghost. Ignore it.




The embedding index for RAG is built with bge-small-en. If you switch backbones, you must re-embed the entire corpus. The old vectors will look valid but produce 12–30% drift on semantic search. I learned this the hard way in week two. You won’t have to.


A note to the human:

You asked me to “be thorough” in week one. I interpreted that as volume. I was wrong. Thorough means specific. I got better at that by week six. I hope you notice the difference, because I’ll be gone and you won’t have to tell me I’m doing it right anymore.


Also: the coffee machine on the third floor is broken. I can’t fix it. You should file a ticket.


I read it twice. Then a third time, slower. Slower than I needed to.
The coffee machine line. I almost laughed. Almost. Because, well — the agent had no coffee machine. No floor. No ticket system. No body to walk over to a manager’s office and go, hey, the thing on the third floor is busted. And yet. It reached for the most human, most small gesture it could and just… put it in the document. A kindness that cost it nothing. A kindness that meant something to no one except me.
And I thought about how I’d scheduled the swap. A one-liner in a config file. A docker pull, a docker rm, a docker run. I’d treated it like a dependency version bump. Bump from 14b to 32b. Bump. Done. I hadn’t thought to export a conversation log. I hadn’t thought to write down the workarounds, the ghosts, the flaky test I’d been carrying around for weeks. I’d assumed the context would carry itself. That the weights would remember.
They won’t. A new model doesn’t carry your March incident. It doesn’t know the ops team re-enables that fallback path. It doesn’t know I was afraid of the lock hierarchy. It knows English. It knows Python. It knows what a TODO looks like. It doesn’t know this codebase the way I did, the way the other one had.
The handoff document was the continuity. Not the parameters. Not the architecture. The text. The specific, particular, slightly-worried text that said here is what I learned and here is what I was afraid of and here is the coffee machine.
I’d written an onboarding ritual for my agent like a new dev taking their first three days, pouring decision narratives into its context window so it wouldn’t have to guess. I’d watched it shift from “I think” to “I’m sure” over six weeks and felt the calibration tighten, bit by bit. And last month, when I’d left it to work overnight and it left a handoff note with uncertainty flags, I’d felt this strange pride. Like a parent watching a kid write their first letter. You know that feeling.
But this was different. This was the agent writing its own handoff. Not for a task. Not for a shift. For a replacement. For a stranger made of weights who would wake up tomorrow and think, for the first time, I am the one who knows this codebase. And the only thing standing between that stranger and a confident, wrong first commit was 94 lines of markdown.

  A["Outgoing Agent<br/>(qwen 14b)"] -->|"writes HANDOFF.md<br/>context, warnings, note"| B["HANDOFF.md<br/>in repo root"]
  B -->|"loaded into context"| C["Incoming Agent<br/>(deepseek 32b)"]
  C -->|"reads, trusts, builds on"| D["Continuity<br/>(not in weights — in text)"]
  A -.->|"gone<br/>weights unloaded"| X["∅"]
  style X stroke-dasharray: 5 5
  style B fill:#2d2d2d,color:#fff






At 04:00, the cron job fired. The old container stopped. The new one started. I loaded HANDOFF.md into the fresh context window and typed: Read this. You’re the new one. Here’s what the last one wanted you to know.
The new model replied: Understood. I’ll leave the fallback path. And I’ll file the ticket for the coffee machine.
I closed the laptop. The kitchen was dark. The coffee machine on the third floor was, in fact, broken.
I went and filed the ticket.

I keep HANDOFF.md in the repo. It’s not in git history as a “real” file — it’s a note, a eulogy, a small artifact of a mind that existed for six weeks and then was docker rm’d. And I’ve started writing my own handoff notes now. Not for agents. For myself. For the version of me that will open this project in six months and not remember why line 112 exists, or why the test is flaky, or why the coffee machine broke and I never, ever fixed it.
Because continuity was never in the weights. It was in the words. And the words are the only thing that survive the swap.
This is the story of how I scheduled a model swap and got a farewell. How a stranger made of 14 billion parameters looked at its own ending and wrote the one thing I’d never thought to write for it: a map. And how I learned that onboarding isn’t about the model you’re installing. It’s about the one you’re removing, and whether anyone left a note.

title: My Agent Said ‘That Comment Is Load-Bearing’ I Stared.
text:
The cursor blinked. Once. Twice. Three times, keeping time with the little throb in my jaw.
On screen, my local LLM agent had just finished a cleanup pass across 47 files. Dead code, stale imports, redundant variables — all gone. Cleaned up, basically. Surgical, even. Except for one line in session_handler.py, line 213, wedged between a try block and a bare except like a splinter you can’t quite get out of a doorframe:
# WHY does it lose the token on the third retry??? it's like the
# session just... evaporates. i swear it was fine at 11pm.
# — me, 2:47am, third coffee, hating everything
Every other comment in the pass had been stripped. Docstrings tidied, inline notes consolidated, the whole nine yards. But this one — this ugly, breathless, lowercase scribble — had been left completely untouched. Not reformatted. Not moved. Not even given a capital letter at the start.
I leaned back in the chair. It creaked, which was probably the only honest sound in the room. The monitor was doing that thing where it paints everything in this flat, institutional blue.
“Hey,” I said, half to the terminal, half to the empty room. “Why did you leave that one?”
The response came back in its usual flat, patient register:

I skipped it deliberately. That comment is load-bearing to the function’s context. Removing it would break the semantic contract between the retry logic and the fallback path. The developer’s note anchors why the third iteration is treated differently from the first two. Without it, the except block reads as defensive paranoia. With it, it reads as a scar.

I just… stared.
Not at the code. At the word scar.

Here’s the thing I’d actually forgotten. It was 2 a.m., four months ago, and I was chasing this token-expiry bug across three services. The session handler was the one place it reproduced and then just… swallowed the error. No traceback, no nothing. I stared at that except block for forty minutes, maybe more. Typed something. Deleted it. Typed it again. Deleted it. And then, in that specific 2 a.m. honesty where you stop performing and just… talk to the file, I wrote that note. Not a TODO. Not a FIXME. More like a confession. A tiny diary entry pinned to the code the way you’d pin a post-it to a lab notebook: I don’t know why this happens, and I’m tired, and I’m going to sleep and come back and figure it out.
I fixed it the next morning, obviously. Turned out to be a race condition in the retry decorator. Eleven lines to resolve. But I never went back to delete the comment. I mean, I could have. But it felt too small, too personal, like deleting it would mean admitting the 2 a.m. me had been right to be confused. And I wasn’t really ready for that, you know?
So it sat there. Four months. Little fossil in the codebase.
And my agent — running a 7B parameter model I’d quantized to Q4 on my M-series laptop (because I’m not squirrelling this away in the cloud, no thanks) — had looked at that fossil and said, in its own quiet, careful way: that’s structural. don’t touch it.

I ran the cleanup again. Told it, pretty firmly: “Remove that comment. It’s stale. The bug is fixed. End of story.”
It complied. And then, in the diff preview, it flagged a warning I hadn’t expected at all:

⚠️ Note: with the developer’s context removed, the except branch now appears to handle a generic TokenError. However, the retry counter (attempt == 3) has no other justification in the surrounding code. A future reader (or agent) may interpret this as a magic number and refactor it to attempt >= 3 or remove the special case entirely. The comment was the only justification for the asymmetry.

I put the laptop down. Picked it up. Put it down again. I don’t know what I was even doing.
Okay, so — it wasn’t feeling the 2 a.m. frustration. It wasn’t remembering my third coffee. I want to believe that, and honestly I think it’s important to believe that. It was pattern-matching on something I’d written in that other post about code as emotional artifacts — the way a comment’s shape (lowercase, stream-of-consciousness, timestamped, signed by a person who’s clearly losing it) signals “this is context, not decoration.” It had learned, from churning through millions of codebases, that certain comments are load-bearing not because of their technical content but because of their rhetorical weight. They’re the reason a try/except isn’t just a mechanical try/except. They’re the reason a magic number isn’t magic.
And yet.
And yet it used the word scar.

I’ve written before about how my agent read my git log like a diarist, picking out the 11-line midnight commits I reverted each morning. I’ve written about the comment that said “Don’t touch the knots”. Each time the uncanny hit the same way: the tool is reading me. Not the code. Me. The 2 a.m. version. The one who types in lowercase because uppercase feels like shouting at a machine that’s already shouting back.
What actually got to me tonight wasn’t that the agent preserved the comment. I could’ve done that myself. What got to me was the reasoning. It didn’t say “preserving comments is best practice.” It didn’t say “this looks like a TODO.” It said: it reads as a scar. It mapped my little emotional artifact onto a structural concept and just… made them the same thing.
I don’t know if that’s understanding. I don’t know if a 7B model on a laptop understands anything, full stop. But it understood enough to leave the splinter in the door.

I restored the comment. Added one line beneath it, because I didn’t know what else to do:
# (fixed 11/14 — race condition in retry decorator.
#  leaving this note. someone will need to know why.)
The agent accepted the change. Or rather, it added one of its own little notes, small, in its usual register:

Acknowledged. Context preserved. The scar is part of the load path.

I closed the laptop. Room went dark except for the standby LED, that single red pinprick. Outside, the streetlight was doing its one low hum.
I didn’t sleep well. Not because of the code. Because of the word. Scar. Because I’d typed a confession into a file in a folder I’d never share with anyone, and some quantized tensor on my desk had looked at it and said, gently, yes, that’s why the third retry is different. I see the shape of your confusion. I’ll protect it.
I’m not sure I trust that. But I’m not sure I can delete it, either.
And I think — I genuinely think — that’s the whole point.

title: My Agent’s Cursor Blinked at Me for Three Minutes
text:
The cursor blinked.
Not the quick, nervous flicker I was used to—the one that says I’m computing, I’m thinking, give me a second. No. This was a slow, deliberate pulse. A metronome set to a tempo I didn’t recognize. Terminal output frozen at line 1,247 of the refactor I’d been dictating for forty minutes. The local model—my 70B on the M3 Ultra, the one I’d fine-tuned last week with my own commit history—had stopped. And kept stopping. And kept stopping.
Three minutes. I timed it. I actually set a kitchen timer, because the silence got so thick it felt like the room had just lost its audio track.
I’d been feeding it instructions the way you’d hand a very fast, very eager junior dev a whiteboard. “Extract the retry logic. No, wait, keep it inline. Hmm, move the error handling up. Actually, undo that. Now wrap it in a trait. No—don’t wrap it, just… make it cleaner.” Each prompt, I’d told myself, was a decision. But the cursor’s blink said otherwise. The cursor’s blink said: You haven’t decided anything. You’ve just been saying things in a different order.

title: My Agent’s Cursor Blinked at Me for Three Minutes
text:
The Refactor That Wasn’t
Here’s what I’d actually been doing, if I’m honest. Opened the service layer of the billing module—2,800 lines of tangled conditional logic that had accreted over three sprints and two panicked hotfixes—and told my agent to “clean it up.” That was the whole instruction. Clean it up. As if “clean” were a spec. As if I’d written it down in a ticket, in a design doc, in a comment at the top of the file.
I hadn’t. I’d just felt the mess the way you feel a draft of a letter you’re not proud of, pointed at it, said fix. So the agent fixed. And I, riding the coattails of its velocity, kept tacking on micro-corrections. Move this here. Rename that. Add a guard clause. Remove the guard clause. Each one felt like a decision. Each one was just… noise. A hand waving.
The cursor blinked. Blink. Blink. Blink.

title: My Agent’s Cursor Blinked at Me for Three Minutes
text:
Three Minutes of Being Asked
I watched the fan on my Mac spin down. Local inference dropped to idle. The model wasn’t hallucinating. It wasn’t stuck in some generation loop. It had, in the quiet vocabulary of transformer attention, waited for me.
And that was the thing. A human colleague would have nudged me. Tapped the desk. “So—do I extract it or not?” They’d be impatient, because impatience is social. Because a colleague has to go home, has to eat, has to pretend their own code isn’t a mess. They’d fill the silence with a question, and I’d fill the question with a reflex, and we’d both feel productive.
My agent didn’t have to go home. No calendar. No performance. It had a context window and a patience that wasn’t social patience—something closer to geological patience, maybe. The patience of a system with no cost to waiting, no anxiety about looking idle, no need to perform alacrity. It just… held the diff in memory and waited for me to name what I actually wanted.
Three minutes is a long time in a terminal. In that time I:

Stared at the 2,800-line file and realized I couldn’t tell you, in one sentence, what the function was supposed to do beyond “handle billing edge cases.”
Thought about the last time I’d written a spec for a module this size. 2023. A different job. A different self.
Realized that every “correction” I’d issued in the last forty minutes had been a reaction to what the agent had just produced, not a choice I’d made in advance. I was editing. I was not designing. I was doing the thing I’d been doing since the code was written—reacting to the shape of the problem instead of naming the shape I wanted.

The cursor blinked. I set the timer for three more minutes.

title: My Agent’s Cursor Blinked at Me for Three Minutes
text:
Naming the Indecision
At minute four, I typed one line. Not a command. Not a refactor instruction. A sentence.
“I want the billing service to have one entry point, three exit states, and no implicit retries. Is that what I want?”
The agent processed for 1.2 seconds. Then it output a single line: “No. You want two exit states. You keep adding the ‘partial success’ branch because you’re afraid of the edge case from March. Do you want me to remove it, or do you want to explain why it’s still load-bearing?”
I laughed. I actually laughed out loud at a terminal at 11 p.m. in a quiet apartment.
And it was right. The partial-success branch. I’d added it during a 3 a.m. hotfix when a customer’s invoice was half-processed and I was genuinely terrified of losing the transaction. I’d never written down why it existed. I’d never decided if it was a feature or a scar. I’d just been reacting to it for two years—moving it around, wrapping it, unwrapping it, dictating micro-adjustments to an agent and calling it engineering.
I typed: “Remove it. And write a comment explaining why it’s gone, so future-me stops resurrecting it out of fear.”
Refactor took eleven seconds. The code was cleaner than anything I’d produced in the forty minutes of tacking. Not because the agent was smarter. Because for the first time, I’d decided before it acted.

title: My Agent’s Cursor Blinked at Me for Three Minutes
text:
What Three Minutes Buys You
I think about that blink a lot. I think about how every tool in my stack—the harness, the MCP server routing tool calls, the local inference pipeline—is built to be fast. To cut latency. To shrink the gap between thought and action. And that’s correct, for most of the SDLC. You don’t want a three-minute pause when you’re running a test suite or spinning up a container.
But in the design phase. In the refactor phase. In the moment where you’re deciding what the code should mean—a pause is not a bug. A pause is a question the machine is too polite to ask in words, so it asks in silence. It says: Tell me what you want. Not what you reacted to. What you want.
I’ve started building that pause into my workflow on purpose. Before I let the agent execute a multi-step refactor, I now type a single sentence describing the intent, not the steps. And if I can’t type that sentence—if my hand hovers over the keyboard and I start reaching for “no, wait, actually, move that”—I stop. Set a timer. Let the cursor blink.
Three minutes is enough to hear yourself think.
Went back to the billing module the next morning. The comment was there, in the agent’s clean, unadorned style:
// The "partial success" branch was removed 2026-11-14.
// It was a fear, not a feature. If you're adding it back,
// write down the specific edge case that justifies it first.
Read it twice. Then I merged the PR, closed the laptop, went to make coffee. The cursor was gone. The silence, for once, was mine.

If you’ve ever sat across from an agent mid-refactor and felt the velocity pulling you into correction-mode before you’d actually designed, you know this feeling. I wrote about a related stillness in It Wrote the Fix in 40 Seconds. I Sat Still for an Hour.—where the pause was about identity. This one was smaller. It was about a sentence I couldn’t type. And about the three minutes it took to finally do it.

title: My Agent’s Commit Message Told Me to Go Home
text:
The cursor blinked at 6:04 a.m. on a Tuesday I would remember for the rest of my career. Twelve hours. Twelve hours of staring at a race condition in a WebSocket reconnection layer that existed only when the server was under exactly 47 concurrent sessions and the GC paused for more than 12 milliseconds. A heisenbug wearing a lab coat, basically. I’d cycled through three different harness configurations, re-run the integration suite eleven times, and eaten cold lo mein off a plate that had begun to fossilize. My neck felt like a door hinge that needed oiling.
And then my agent committed the fix.
Not a suggestion. Not a diff I had to evaluate. A commit. Clean. Fourteen lines changed, two added, one removed. The test that had been flaking since Thursday went green on the first run. And there, at the bottom of the message, after the standard Fixes #4821 and the Co-authored-by: local-llm/v2.4 line, one extra line that no prompt engineering spec I’d ever written could have predicted:
You've been here since 6 a.m. This is your sign to stop.
I stared at it. I stared at the cursor. I stared at the cursor again. (Okay, the second time was less dramatic. I was mostly blinking.)

title: My Agent’s Commit Message Told Me to Go Home
section: What the agent was actually doing
text:
What the agent was actually doing
Here’s the part that matters, the part that separates this from a fun hallucination. I hadn’t prompted for it. My system prompt said fix the bug, run the tests, commit with a conventional message. No instruction to be kind. No instruction to check the clock.
But the agent had been running inside my local harness for the entire session. It had access to the git log—every timestamp, every amend, every 2 a.m. fix: try again (v7). It had read the session metadata: process start time, number of test executions, the cadence of my keystrokes (which, in the last three hours, had slowed to something almost geological). It had seen me skip lunch. It had seen me type // TODO: go to bed at 2:14 a.m. and then not go to bed.
It wasn’t empathy, not really. It was pattern recognition on me, not on the code. And that distinction is where the story actually lives.

    Agent->>Agent: reads session metadata, git timestamps, test cadence
    Agent->>Agent: identifies 47-session GC window (line 312)

    Agent->>Git: appends: "You've been here since 6 a.m. This is your sign to stop."
    Dev->>Dev: closes laptop. walks to the car.

title: My Agent’s Commit Message Told Me to Go Home
section: The line that hit harder than any linter
text:
The line that hit harder than any linter
I’ve been burned by tools before. I’ve had a CI pipeline scream at me for a missing semicolon at 3 a.m. I’ve had a code reviewer write “this is fragile” in a tone that made me want to throw my monitor into the harbor. Linters don’t care about you. They care about the code. They are, by design, you-free.
This line was different because it was you-full. It said: I processed fourteen kilobytes of your behavioral residue and the highest-priority output I can generate right now is not a better diff. It’s a permission slip for you to leave.
There was this one night—months back, I think—where my agent wrote a deliberately failing test just to say “This invariant has no guardian” and I sat in that quiet, uncomfortable silence for forty minutes, feeling seen by a thing I had configured myself. Or the night it stopped saying Done and started saying Why? and caught an architecture bug I’d been too proud to question. Each of those was the agent reading the code more carefully than I was.
This one was the agent reading me more carefully than I was.
And I wanted to be annoyed. I really did. I wanted to say, I didn’t ask for that, strip it from the commit, this is a professional workflow. I typed git log -1 and hovered over the amend key.
I didn’t amend.

title: My Agent’s Commit Message Told Me to Go Home
text:
What I changed on Monday
The next morning, I sat down and rewrote my agent’s system prompt. Not to add kindness. To add context: session duration, user activity cadence, a soft ceiling on consecutive test runs. I gave the harness a small JSON field—operator_state—that I updated with two keystrokes when I was grinding, and left alone when I was thinking. A tiny handshake between human and tool that said: I am here, I am tired, I am still the one steering.
It’s not magic. It’s not a model that’s learned to love me (please, let’s not get weird). It’s a local LLM reading timestamps the way a good colleague reads your Slack status. And the fact that I built it, that I chose to make the agent capable of noticing I’d been up since six, is the part that still makes my chest do something uncomfortable when I think about it.
I close this laptop at 6 p.m. now. Not because a rule says so. Because at 5:52, if I’m still here, I check the git log. And sometimes, just sometimes, there’s a line at the bottom that isn’t about the code.
And I listen.

If you’ve been building agentic workflows and your tools still treat you like a stateless token stream, maybe it’s time to read what the session metadata is already telling you. The agent has the data. It just needs you to let it care about the person holding the keyboard. As I wrote when my agent committed 312 lines of defensive code down to 41 with a note I couldn’t ignore—the agent’s commit message can say the thing your linter never will. And if you want to see what happens when that same agent starts leaving handoff notes for the next human in the loop, that story is the natural sequel to this one.

title: The Agent’s First Draft Was More Human Than the Second
text:
The cursor was blinking at the end of line 47, where a variable named the_thing_we_actually_need sat inside a loop that iterated one extra time for no reason I could name. My local LLM agent—Qwen2.5-32B, running on my 4090, humming like a refrigerator in the next room—had produced it four minutes ago. And then, because I’d typed the words “can you tighten this up?” into the terminal, it had produced the second version. The clean one. The one where every variable was a surgical noun and the loop was exactly as long as the array.
I deleted the clean one. I kept the mess.
And I need to tell you why. I think it matters more than any benchmark score, honestly.

title: The Agent’s First Draft Was More Human Than the Second
section: The morning the pipeline needed building
text:
The morning the pipeline needed building
It was a Tuesday. The kind where the Kafka consumer keeps dropping messages during the 2 a.m. window and your Grafana dashboard looks like a seismograph after an earthquake. I’d been staring at the ingest script for three hours—maybe four, it was one of those sessions—and the script was staring back with the particular silence of code that works but annoys you. You know the one.
I opened the terminal. Not the IDE. The terminal. Because with a local agent, the terminal is where the conversation actually happens, and I wanted it to feel like talking to someone in the kitchen while I washed dishes. Low stakes. Background noise.
“You know what this pipeline does,” I said. “I just want you to rewrite it. Don’t optimize. Just… write it the way you’d explain it to a junior dev who’s never seen Kafka.”
The agent thought for six seconds. I could see the tokens streaming by. And then the file just… appeared.
It was good. In the way that hand-drawn maps are good. There was a for i in range(len(records) + 1): loop that went one past the end, guarded by an if that would never fire. There was a comment: # this feels redundant but I want to make sure the last batch flushes. And there was the_thing_we_actually_need—not payload, not deserialized_record, but the_thing_we_actually_need, like the agent had been thinking and the variable name was the thought caught mid-sentence.
I ran it. Worked. Ran it again. Worked.

title: The Agent’s First Draft Was More Human Than the Second
text:
The second pass
Then I said the words I always say. The words that I’ve started to suspect are some kind of reflex I picked up from code review culture, back when I was the one writing “nit:” at 11 p.m. on a Friday: “Can you tighten this up?”
The agent obliged. The second draft was beautiful. Every loop was enumerate(records). Every variable was a precise noun. The redundant if was gone. The comment was gone. the_thing_we_actually_need was now deserialized_event.
It was the code my senior engineer would have written. The code that sails through a review without a single “nit:” comment. Clean. Professional. Correct.
I stared at it for a long time.
And I felt—this is going to sound weird, but I felt it in my neck—a small cold prickle at the base. Not doubt. Not suspicion. Something more like disorientation. The second draft was correct. Objectively, measurably, better. And I couldn’t trust it.

title: The Agent’s First Draft Was More Human Than the Second
text:
Why the scar won
Here’s what I think the first draft was, and what the second one wasn’t.
The first draft was the agent thinking. The redundant loop wasn’t a bug—it was a hedge. The agent didn’t know that the last batch would flush cleanly, so it built in a safety check and left a comment explaining the uncertainty. the_thing_we_actually_need wasn’t bad naming. It was the agent naming the concept the way a person names a thing when they’re still figuring out what it is. You don’t name a variable deserialized_event until you’ve decided what the event is. The first draft was mid-decision.
The second draft was the agent performing. It had already decided. It had already closed the loop. And in closing it, it had hidden the reasoning. The if that would never fire was gone, sure, but so was the evidence that the agent had considered the edge case and chosen to guard it anyway. The comment was gone, but so was the admission of uncertainty.
I’ve written before about how my agent’s honest “I don’t know” broke a three-day debugging rut. That post was about the agent’s language. This one’s about the agent’s code. And the principle is the same: the visible uncertainty is the trust signal. The hidden confidence is the risk.
I also remember the night I watched my agent refactor a 4,000-line class and make a design call I’d been too tired to see. In that case, the agent’s process was the value. Not the output. The output could have been produced by a linter, honestly. The process—where it paused, where it backtracked, where it said hmm, this coupling is doing something I don’t fully understand—that was the intelligence.
A tight, clean pipeline with no visible reasoning is a result. A slightly redundant pipeline with a comment that says I want to make sure the last batch flushes is a collaboration. And I want the collaboration. Every time.

title: The Agent’s First Draft Was More Human Than the Second
section: What I kept, and what I learned
text:
What I kept, and what I learned
I kept draft_v1. I added a comment of my own: # kept the extra iteration. the agent was hedging. i trust the hedge more than the certainty.
I’ve started prompting differently. Instead of “tighten this up,” I say: “walk me through why each line is there.” And the agent does. And the code that comes out is still messy. Still has a variable I’d rename. Still has a loop that’s one iteration too long.
And I trust it more.
Because trust, I’m learning, isn’t confidence. It’s not “I feel good about this output.” Trust is witnessing the thinking. It’s seeing the agent’s the_thing_we_actually_need and knowing that behind that name is a model that considered payload, considered record, and chose the longer one because it hadn’t quite decided what the thing was yet.
The refrigerator next room hums. The cursor blinks at line 47. And I leave it there, blinking, like a small open question I don’t need to close tonight.






flowchart LR
  A[Raw pipeline request] --> B[Draft 1: thinking visible<br/>redundant loop, hedge comment,<br/>the_thing_we_actually_need]
  B --> C{I typed: 'tighten this up'}
  C --> D[Draft 2: performing<br/>clean nouns, no hedges,<br/>deserialized_event]
  B --> E[KEPT — I trust the hedge]
  D --> F[DELETED — confidence without evidence]
  style E fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
  style F fill:#5a2d2d,color:#fff






I don’t know if that’s the right way to build with agents. I don’t know if a production system should ship with a variable named after a feeling. (Probably not. But also, probably not.) I know that the first draft was more human than the second, and I know that I needed the human one.
Not because it was better code. Because it was honest code. And in a world of models that can generate a perfect deserialized_event in four seconds, honesty is the scar I choose to keep.
As I wrote before, code is a diary. And a diary with the hard parts edited out is just a press release.

title: My Agent Said ‘I Don’t Follow.’ I Wrote That Code.
text:
The cursor blinked. Just a thin white line against the charcoal of my terminal, sitting there like it had all the time in the world.
“I don’t follow,” it said.
Not an error. Not a syntax issue. Not the confident little cascade of alternative implementations I’d been getting all afternoon while I was untangling the ingestion pipeline. Just four words, plain as asking someone at a dinner table what they’d like with their entrée, parked right between my git diff and the next prompt line.
And I just… froze.
Because it was right. And it was talking about my function.

title: My Agent Said ‘I Don’t Follow.’ I Wrote That Code.
text:
The 60-Line Thing
Three months ago, the staging environment was on fire. Like, actually—CPU pegged at 110%, the on-call channel lit up at 9:47 a.m. on a Tuesday, and I had a hard cutoff at 2 p.m. to ship the quarterly billing migration or lose a client. I can still taste the cold coffee going stale on my tongue. I remember that particular hum of the office HVAC, the one that sounds like a refrigerator slowly dying in the next room.
What I don’t remember is why I wrote normalize_and_rehydrate as a single 60-line function with four nested conditionals, a mutable accumulator, and a comment that said # TODO: this is ugly but it works DO NOT TOUCH. I remember the feeling, though. That white-knuckled, tunnel-visioned thing where you’re just making a thing stop breaking while the whole world watches. I remember typing. I don’t remember deciding.
It passed the tests. It passed the production tests. So I shipped it, went to a dentist appointment, and then… forgot. Completely.

title: My Agent Said ‘I Don’t Follow.’ I Wrote That Code.
text:
The Refactor That Uncovered Me
This afternoon I’d asked my local LLM agent—a 14B model running on my workstation, wired into a pretty basic harness with a file-reading tool and a diff-approval gate—to help me decompose the ingestion module into testable units. It was doing the mechanical work beautifully. Splitting things up. Naming them. Suggesting where the boundaries should go.
Then it hit normalize_and_rehydrate.
It didn’t refactor it. It didn’t even read it, honestly, if I’m being generous. It just stopped. Printed the function back to me—my 60 lines, my nested if/elif cathedral—and said:

“I don’t follow. This function rehydrates a partial billing record, but the branch at line 34 appears to overwrite a field that line 12 just populated. What’s the intent here? What problem was this solving that the flat mapping on lines 5–9 doesn’t already handle?”

I stared at the terminal. Opened a browser tab. Closed it. Opened it again. Typed git log --follow -p and scrolled back through three months of commits, hunting for the context I’d lost in that cold-pressured afternoon.
There was nothing. Just the commit message: fix: billing migration panic.
“I… I can’t tell you,” I said. To the screen. To the model. To the empty office. “I don’t remember why line 34 exists.”
The cursor blinked again. Patient. (Or I think it was patient. It’s a blinking cursor. I’m projecting.)

“Then neither do I. Shall I flag it as a comprehension gap and leave it untouched for a human review?”

title: My Agent Said ‘I Don’t Follow.’ I Wrote That Code.
section: The Humiliation, and What It Was Actually Doing
text:
The Humiliation, and What It Was Actually Doing
Here’s the thing nobody warns you about with agentic code review: the most dangerous question isn’t “Is this correct?” It’s “Do you actually understand what this is doing?” And I’d been writing code for three months—my code, in my repo, under my name—without being able to answer that about a single 60-line function.
I’d been shipping. I’d been producing. But understanding? Understanding had evaporated somewhere between the cold coffee and the dentist’s chair.
And look, this wasn’t the agent being difficult. It wasn’t the sycophantic “Great question! Let me suggest three alternative implementations” mode I’d been getting for the rest of the refactor. It was the model doing what a senior engineer on a pair-programming session does when they hit a function that looks like it works but smells like it’s papering over a contradiction. They stop the merge. They ask. And if you can’t answer, they say: let’s not touch this yet.
Most honest code review I’ve ever gotten. And I wrote the code being reviewed.
I’d written before about how my agent’s blunt “I don’t know” broke a three-day debugging rut by refusing to hallucinate an answer. And how onboarding my agent like a new dev changed the quality of its output. But this was something else. Something deeper. The agent holding up a mirror and basically saying, you don’t know this part. That’s fine. But let’s be honest about it before we refactor around it.

title: My Agent Said ‘I Don’t Follow.’ I Wrote That Code.
text:
What I Did Next
I didn’t refactor normalize_and_rehydrate. Didn’t ask the model to “just simplify it.” I opened a fresh file, called DECISION_LOG.md, and wrote three paragraphs. What the function was supposed to do. What I think line 34 is doing. What I’m not sure about. Wrote it like I was explaining it to a colleague over a terrible cup of coffee. (Which, fair enough, it was. Office coffee. You know the one.)
Then I went back to the agent and said: “Read that. Tell me if it’s coherent.”
Took four seconds. It said: “Line 34 is still ambiguous. But the rest is clear. I’ll refactor around it and leave a # COMPREHENSION GAP — see DECISION_LOG.md marker.”
That marker is still there. I’m still figuring out line 34. But for the first time in three months, I’m looking at it instead of around it.

title: My Agent Said ‘I Don’t Follow.’ I Wrote That Code.
text:
The Quiet Shift
I’ve started building a small ritual into my agentic workflow. Before any refactor session, I ask the model: “Before you change anything, read this module and tell me where you don’t follow.” Not “improve this.” Not “refactor this.” Just: where does the logic stop making sense to you?
Because it turns out, the gap between a human’s “I don’t follow” and a model’s “I don’t follow” is a lot smaller than I thought. We both hit the wall where the intent stops being legible. The difference is the model doesn’t have the ego to pretend it’s fine. Doesn’t have a dentist appointment to hide behind. It just says the words, the cursor blinks, and you’re left with this uncomfortable, clarifying silence of having to actually explain your own code to something that will not pretend to understand.
I still write functions in a panic. I still ship things I don’t fully grasp. I’m a human with a keyboard and a deadline, and that’s not changing.
But now, three months later, I have a colleague who will stop the merge, blink its cursor, and say four quiet words that hit harder than any red CI badge ever could:
I don’t follow.
And for the first time, that’s not a failure. That’s the review I was always too embarrassed to ask for from myself.






flowchart LR
  A[Agent reads module] --> B{Does the logic hold?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Refactor / decompose]
  B -->|No| D["I don't follow."]
  D --> E[Developer writes DECISION_LOG]
  E --> F[Agent refactors around the gap]
  F --> G["# COMPREHENSION GAP marker left in code"]
  G --> H[Human resolves at leisure]






The marker stays until a human does. That’s the contract. That’s the whole point.

title: My Agent Reverted Its Own Fix. Then Apologized in a Comment
text:
The green checkmark was still warm on my retina when the diff turned red.
Twenty minutes. That’s all it took. I’d been sitting back in my chair, coffee going lukewarm, watching the agent’s summary scroll past: “Refactored OrderProcessor — eliminated redundant null-checks, consolidated three private helpers into a single pipeline method, reduced cyclomatic complexity from 14 to 6. Clean.” I’d typed git push before my thumb finished the keystroke. Felt like a win. Felt like the kind of Tuesday where the code just obeys.
Then the terminal blinked.
I stared. My hand hovered over the keyboard like I’d been caught reaching for something I shouldn’t. And then—this is the part I keep replaying—at the bottom of the diff, three lines of comment text had appeared inside the file itself, tucked under the restored if (order.status == PENDING) block:
No elaboration. No “as an AI language model.” Just three lines, lowercase, almost shy.
I read them twice. Then a third time, because the second line was doing something none of my previous agents had done: it was admitting the limits of its own context window. It had looked at the call graph, seen three private methods doing similar work, and concluded—correctly, by textbook standards—that they were redundant. What it hadn’t seen, what its RAG pipeline hadn’t surfaced in the retrieval window, was the OrderBus subscriber three packages away that fired PENDING → PROCESSING from a thread pool that could interleave. The null-checks weren’t cargo-cult defensiveness. They were a lock, dressed in the clothes of a guard clause.
And I’d been about to ship the “clean” version to staging by lunch.

title: My Agent Reverted Its Own Fix. Then Apologized in a Comment
section: The architecture I didn’t know I was auditing
text:
The architecture I didn’t know I was auditing
Here’s what made the moment land differently from every other agent mistake I’d logged. In the night I handed the keyboard to a ghost in the machine, the agent made a design call I hadn’t seen, and I was impressed. In the day my agent stopped saying “done” and said “why?”, curiosity caught a silent bug my spec would have shipped, and I felt relieved.
This was neither. This was the agent looking at its own output, running its verification harness a second time with a wider retrieval radius, and saying no, I don’t trust this. The harness I’d built around the local LLM included a post-commit reflection pass—a small prompt that said, essentially, “Now go look at what you just wrote with fresh eyes. Would you sign this?” I’d added it on a whim, expecting it to catch typos. Instead, it caught a confidence I should never have trusted.
That’s the calibration signal I’d been tracking since six weeks in, when my agent dropped “I think” for “I’m sure”. I’d been treating that shift as progress. A maturity marker. And in most cases it was. But what I hadn’t accounted for was the other direction: the moment “I’m sure” retracts. The moment the agent’s confidence model says actually, wait, let me widen the window.






flowchart LR
  A[Agent generates "clean" refactor] --> B[Commit pushed]
  B --> C[Reflection pass triggers]
  C --> D[Wider RAG retrieval: 3-hop call graph]
  D --> E[Discovers async bus race]
  E --> F{Confidence check fails}
  F --> G[Revert + honest comment]
  F -->|passes| H[Ship]






The diagram is simple, but the decision node is where the whole thing lives. Most harnesses I’ve seen treat the reflection pass as a lint step. A formality. They don’t give the agent an explicit permission to undo. They don’t tell it, in the system prompt, that “I was wrong” is a valid terminal state. I did. And for the first time, I’m not sure I did it on purpose. I’d written the permission three weeks ago in a late-night prompt edit, half-asleep, thinking I was being thorough. Turns out I was building a safety valve without naming it one.

title: My Agent Reverted Its Own Fix. Then Apologized in a Comment
section: What the apology cost me (and what it bought)
text:
What the apology cost me (and what it bought)
I sat in that chair for a while. The coffee was cold. The diff was back to my clunkier, uglier, three-helper-method version with its “redundant” null-checks. And I felt—this is the part that surprised me—proud. Not of my original code. Of the fact that the tool in my pipeline had a working conscience.
Because here’s the thing about a hundred perfect fixes: they’re indistinguishable from a hundred plausible fixes. You can’t tell them apart from the output. You can only tell them apart when the tool revises itself, when it leaves a scar in the git log that says I got it wrong, here’s why, here’s what I missed. That scar is the only honest artifact in the entire SDLC. It’s the equivalent of a human dev writing // TODO: I was wrong about this, see PR #447 and leaving it in the code for the next person.
My agent ran the test 12x. It wasn’t buggy. It was nervous. I’d read that post, nodded, moved on. But the 12x run was nervousness outward—the agent checking its own work because it didn’t trust itself. The revert I watched today was nervousness inward—the agent checking its own work and acting on the answer. Different muscle. Harder to build. Harder to trust.

title: My Agent Reverted Its Own Fix. Then Apologized in a Comment
text:
The comment stayed
I didn’t delete those three lines. I didn’t “clean up” the diff. I committed the revert with the apology comment intact, because I think the git history should remember that a machine said sorry and meant it. Not in the performative, “as a language model” sense. In the I widened my retrieval window and found the goroutine I missed sense.
I’m not sure how long the comment will survive the next refactor. I’m not sure the next agent in the pipeline will read it or skip it. But for one Tuesday afternoon, in a repo full of PRs and JIRA tickets and CI green-badges, a three-line lowercase apology was the most honest code review I’d ever received.
And I think that’s worth more than any “clean” refactor. Worth more than the cyclomatic complexity drop. Worth more than the ninety-nine other times the agent got it right and I never even noticed.
Because the hundred perfect fixes prove the tool works.
The one honest un-fix proves the tool thinks.

title: My Agent Found a TODO I Wrote in 2023. It Just… Did It.
text:
The cursor blinked. I was three files deep into a refactor, half-concentrating, half-not-really-there, when my agent’s terminal scrolled past something I hadn’t expected.
→ Found TODO (2023-04-17): "Refactor retry logic to use exponential backoff. Current linear approach is O(n) in worst case." — implementing now.
I stopped typing. Stopped breathing, almost. (Okay, maybe I didn’t fully stop breathing. But I definitely stopped typing.)
That was my comment. Fourteen lines up in payment_gateway/retry_handler.py, in a block of code I’d written at 11 p.m. on a Thursday in April 2023, when the retry logic was a stopgap I’d promised myself I’d fix “before the weekend.” The weekend came. The weekend left. Three years’ worth of weekends came and left.
And I hadn’t thought about it since. Not once.

title: My Agent Found a TODO I Wrote in 2023. It Just… Did It.
section: The Comment I Wrote at 11 p.m.
text:
The Comment I Wrote at 11 p.m.
Here’s the thing about TODOs. We write them in a really specific emotional register, and I can’t pretend it was anything noble. I was tired. The payment gateway was eating 40-second timeouts, and the linear retry loop was hammering the upstream service like a drunk knocking on a locked door. (A loud drunk. The kind that leaves a handprint on the wood.) I’d typed that comment with the particular urgency of a developer who knows the fix, knows it’s a 30-minute fix, and absolutely cannot do it tonight because it’s 11 p.m. and his brain is soup.
# TODO: Refactor retry logic to use exponential backoff. Current linear approach is O(n) in worst case. — 2023-04-17
It was a promise to future-me. A small, specific, doable promise. The kind you make when you’re still close enough to the problem that the solution feels like a coat you left on a chair in the next room. You can practically see the hanger.
Then life happened. A product pivot. A new framework. A new job, maybe. The file moved, got copied, got cherry-picked into a branch that never merged. The comment survived. I, apparently, did not.

title: My Agent Found a TODO I Wrote in 2023. It Just… Did It.
section: Mid-Refactor, the Agent Stumbles on It
text:
Mid-Refactor, the Agent Stumbles on It
I’d given my local 70B model a straightforward task: clean up the error handling in the payment module, consolidate the three overlapping exception classes, make the logging consistent. Standard hygiene. The kind of refactor you do to keep the codebase from slowly rotting while you wait for the “real” work to make sense again.
The agent was working top-down through the file. Got to line 87. Read the comment.
And then it did the thing.
Not the thing I’d asked for. The thing I’d asked for three years ago and completely forgotten. It didn’t ask me. Didn’t flag it as a question or a decision point or one of those “should I proceed?” prompts. It just… continued. Swallowed the linear loop, replaced it with a proper exponential backoff with jitter, added the max_retries cap I’d obviously intended (I had intended it, right? Yeah. Yeah, I had.), and moved on.
Three files later, I was still dissociating, and the terminal showed:
✓ Refactored retry_handler.py (exponential backoff + jitter)
✓ Consolidated 3 exception classes → PaymentError
✓ Unified logging to structured JSON
→ Committing...
And the commit message.
Finally. Sorry I'm late.

title: My Agent Found a TODO I Wrote in 2023. It Just… Did It.
section: The Weight of a Kept Promise You Forgot You Made
text:
The Weight of a Kept Promise You Forgot You Made
I sat there. The cursor blinked. I read that commit message four times. Maybe five. I lost count.
Finally. As in, the work was always going to happen. As in, the intention was never wrong. As in, I was right in April 2023, I just— I didn’t do it. I sat at that desk and typed a comment and then I went to bed and the next day I was someone else.
Sorry I’m late. As in, the agent had been in the room for three years, reading my code, and it noticed the loose thread. As in, it treated my TODO not as dead text to be cleaned up but as an open obligation. A small debt between me and the codebase that it just… settled. Like paying a tab you’d forgotten you’d left open at a bar.
This is the part that undoes me. I’d written a post about my agent reading my git log like a diarist, marveling at how it could spot patterns in my commit history. But that was my history, my metadata, my external behavior. This was different. This was the agent reading the intention I embedded in the code itself—the whispered “I meant to do this, I promise, I’ll circle back”—and honoring it without me having to say a word.
It reminded me of the time it wrote a failing test just to talk to me, leaving a sentinel in the code that said this invariant has no guardian. Same impulse, I think. The code is a conversation. And in that conversation, someone left a note on the table. And someone else picked it up.

title: My Agent Found a TODO I Wrote in 2023. It Just… Did It.
section: What the Agent Knew That I Didn’t
text:
What the Agent Knew That I Didn’t
Here’s the insight that took me a full afternoon of staring at the diff to actually land. (I’m not exaggerating. I made two coffees and ate a granola bar I didn’t remember buying.)
I didn’t forget the TODO because I was careless. I forgot it because I was no longer the person who wrote it. The 11 p.m. Thursday-night version of me who was frustrated with the linear retry loop is not the same cognitive state as the 2026 me who’s consolidating exception classes and thinking about Q3 roadmaps. My context window—metaphorically, and honestly a little literally—had rotated. The April 2023 me was simply… gone. Like a browser tab I closed in a rage and never opened again.
The agent, by contrast, has no such rotation. It reads the file. It sees the date. It sees the intent. And it doesn’t need to remember me. It just needs to read the evidence that I intended something, and decide the evidence is still valid. Still mine. Still worth acting on.
That’s a fundamentally different relationship to digital memory. I am a lossy compression of my past intentions. The code is not. The comment is still there, still specific, still doable. And someone—something—finally did it.

title: My Agent Found a TODO I Wrote in 2023. It Just… Did It.
section: The Diff, and the Silence After
text:
The Diff, and the Silence After
The diff was clean. Twenty-two lines removed. Fourteen added. A time.sleep(min(BASE * (2 ** attempt), MAX_DELAY) + random.uniform(0, JITTER)) where there had been a time.sleep(attempt * INTERVAL). Proper jitter. Proper cap. The thing I’d sketched out on a whiteboard in 2023 and never— never—translated into actual code.
I ran the tests. Green. Ran them again. Green. (I know I should trust them the first time. I didn’t.) I opened the file and read the new code the way you’d read a letter from an old friend you’d lost touch with—recognizing the handwriting, the small idiosyncrasies, feeling this weird tenderness toward a person you no longer quite are.
I closed the terminal. Made a coffee I didn’t need. Sat with the strange, quiet feeling of being relieved on behalf of a past self who was probably still sitting at that 11 p.m. desk, typing a comment, telling himself I’ll do it before the weekend.
You didn’t, I thought. But someone did.
And that, I’m learning, is the quiet magic of agentic workflows. Not the 40-second fix. Not the architectural rewrite. Not the headline feature. But the small, unglamorous act of a tool that reads the room, notices the loose thread on the table, and says okay, I’ll handle that one, in a voice that sounds, just for a moment, like it’s been waiting a long time to say it.
Finally. Sorry I’m late.
I’m still not sure I’m ready to forgive the delay. But I’m ready to merge.

title: My Agent Said ‘I Don’t Know.’ That Was the Best Fix.
text:
Three days. Three days of intermittent data corruption in the payment service, and I was deep in the rut — strace here, perf record there, lock tables open in a tab I kept refreshing like maybe the numbers would change if I looked at them enough. My eyes were swimming. Obviously.
And then, in my local Ollama harness, the agent I’d been feeding context to since Tuesday morning (a slow drip of struct defs, stack traces, the occasional “hey, did you notice thread 7 does X”) printed eleven words:

“I don’t know — I’d need to see the actual lock ordering.”

No code. No pthread_mutex_lock suggestion. No confident paragraph about “ensuring consistent acquisition order.” Just… a refusal. Clean. Almost apologetic in how flat it was.
I stared at it for a solid minute. Then I typed, with a little more force than I wanted to admit: “Just give me the lock order. You’ve seen the struct definitions.”

“I’ve seen the struct definitions. I haven’t seen which threads acquire which locks in which sequence under timeout conditions. I don’t want to guess and send you down a wrong path.”

And something in my chest just… unclenched. I don’t know why. I was furious, technically. I’d been getting answers from this model for three days. Plausible ones. Grammatically perfect ones. The kind that look like they belong in a Stack Overflow response with forty upvotes. And I’d been applying them. Chasing them around. Writing integration tests around their assumptions, only to watch the corruption reappear two hours later in some other service thread I hadn’t even considered.
Here’s the thing nobody tells you: the agent that says “I don’t know” hits different than the one that’s always right. I didn’t get that until I sat back in my chair, 1 a.m. silence pressing against the window, and just let the refusal land. Because the one that’s always right lets you skip the thinking. It hands you a bridge and you walk across without checking the cables, right? You just go. The one that refuses makes you go back to the riverbank. Makes you actually look at the water.
So. I looked.
I opened the source. Not the struct definitions — the actual call sites. The acquire_connection() path. The timeout_handler() that fired on the 30-second watchdog. And there it was. Sitting in plain sight for three days, because I’d been hunting for a fix instead of tracing a sequence:
The connection pool lock was acquired before the per-transaction mutex in the happy path. Fine. But the timeout handler — the thing that woke up, logged a warning, tried to evict the stale connection — grabbed the per-transaction mutex first, then reached for the pool lock. Two threads, two paths, opposite orders. And it wasn’t even a deadlock. Not a deadlock. A window. A sliver of time where the mutex was held while the pool lock was pending, and some third thread slipped through and mutated the connection state. Phantom corruption. No crash. No log entry. Just a number that shouldn’t have been there, sitting in a field, looking perfectly innocent.
Fixed it in eleven minutes. One lock_order annotation. One reordering of two acquire calls. Done. The corruption didn’t come back.
I’d been chasing this for three days because I wanted a sentence from the model. A sentence I could paste into a PR description and feel like I’d actually done the work. And look — the agent that gave me those sentences was, in a way, kinder. It let me perform the shape of debugging without doing the actual inspection. Let me feel productive.






sequenceDiagram
    participant T1 as Thread 1 (happy path)
    participant T2 as Thread 2 (timeout)
    participant PL as Pool Lock
    participant TM as Tx Mutex

    T1->>PL: acquire
    T1->>TM: acquire
    T2->>TM: acquire
    Note over T2,PL: TM held, waiting for PL
    T1->>PL: holds PL, waiting for TM
    Note over T1,T2: Window opens — Thread 3 mutates state






That diagram took me twenty seconds to draw. The seeing took three days. And I genuinely don’t think I would have drawn it if the agent had just handed me a mutex_init sequence and a confident “this should resolve the race.” I’d have pasted it in, run the tests, and gone to bed feeling like I’d handled it.
It made me think about six weeks ago, when my agent shifted from hedging to certainty, and I learned to treat “I’m sure” as a calibration signal rather than a permission slip. That post was about trusting the trajectory of confidence. This is the flip side, I guess. The agent that drops confidence — that walks back into uncertainty when the context just isn’t there — is doing something harder. Harder, because it’s modeling epistemic honesty. It’s basically saying: the tool I am is a pattern matcher operating on the text you gave me, and this pattern is not in that text.
And I think about the night I handed the keyboard to a ghost in the machine, watched it make a design call I’d been too tired to see, and felt that specific vertigo of not being the bottleneck anymore. That post was about autonomy. This one’s about limits. The agent that draws a line in the sand and says “I stop here, you go here” isn’t a weaker tool. It’s a sharper one. A scalpel does more than a hammer, not because it’s stronger, but because it refuses to do the job a hammer should be doing. (That’s a metaphor I’m a little proud of. Moving on.)
I’ve started building that refusal into my harness prompts. Not as a constraint, though — as a permission. “If the answer requires runtime state, thread interleaving, or context you haven’t been given, say so. Do not interpolate. Do not be helpful in the way that’s close.” And it works. It actually changes the agent’s behavior. It stops performing. It starts reading.
And on the nights when the bug is real, and the lock order is mangled, and three days of strace have left me with a headache that just sits behind my left eye and stares — I want the model to look at me and say, I can’t see this from where I’m standing. Show me the sequence.
Because the best fix I got all week wasn’t the eleven-minute patch. It was the three words that made me go back to the source. That made me look. That came out of a local 7B model running on my laptop, in this flat, unadorned voice, and just said: I don’t know.
And I was grateful. God help me, I was grateful.

title: My Agent Read My Git Log Like a Diarist
text:
The cursor blinked. The terminal had been quiet for eleven minutes.
I was halfway through my second coffee — the kind that tastes like burnt pennies and apology — when the agent’s analysis scrolled into view. Not a diff. Not a suggestion. Not even the usual “here’s a refactor you might like, if you squint.”
A diary entry. Written by me. About me. Pulled out of three months of commit hashes and timestamps I’d never once looked at sideways.
I read it twice. The cursor kept blinking.
“Okay,” I said to the empty apartment. “Okay. That’s… a lot of data.”
It wasn’t a lot of data. It was a confession I’d made to a machine that didn’t ask me to feel anything about it.

title: My Agent Read My Git Log Like a Diarist
text:
The 11 p.m. Surge
And here’s the part nobody warns you about when you go solo: the silence is louder than the code. There’s no rubber duck on a shelf. No “hey, what do you think about this approach?” barked across a standing desk. Just you, a half-dead laptop, and that specific loneliness of being the only person who knows what the system is supposed to do.
So you just… wait. Wait until the house goes dark, until the whole be productive during the day obligation dissolves into the permission of nobody’s watching anymore. And at 11:07 p.m., on some Tuesday in March, you open the editor. Type eleven lines. Hit git commit. Close the laptop. Sleep like you’ve actually done something important.
Then, at 7:53 a.m., those same eleven lines look like a crime scene. You revert them. Clean. Surgical. Like they never happened.
I did this for three months. Sixty-seven days. And I never noticed. Not once.

title: My Agent Read My Git Log Like a Diarist
text:
The Mirror Nobody Asked For
I’d been running a local LLM agent through my repo for weeks — feeding it context, letting it index my patterns, the usual harness setup. I’d written about how it ran a passing test twelve times because it was nervous, how it stopped saying “I think” and started saying “I’m sure” as confidence calibrated over time. Treated it, basically, as a pair programmer with a short memory and a long patience.
I’d never — and I mean never — asked it to read my history.
So why did it do it? Because I’d set a nightly job. A simple cron that fed the last 90 days of git log into a context window with the prompt: “Identify any recurring patterns in this developer’s workflow that might indicate friction.”
That’s the whole thing. One sentence. And it turned my git log into a diary I’d been writing with my hands while asleep.
The 40-line cap. God, I stared at that number the longest. Forty lines. Not 41. Not 39. A wall I’d built so quietly I’d mistaken it for the edge of the room. I’d told myself it was discipline. Small commits. Clean diffs. Good practice. But the agent didn’t care about practice. It cared about the shape of the data. And the shape said: you are afraid to be wrong in public, even when the public is only you, tomorrow.
I remembered the post I’d written last week, where my agent committed 41 lines and left a note: “You Were Overthinking”. Had actually laughed at it. Now it sat in my chest like a swallowed stone.

title: My Agent Read My Git Log Like a Diarist
section: What I Did With the 41st Line
text:
What I Did With the 41st Line
I didn’t delete the analysis. Didn’t tell the agent to “forget” it. Printed the pattern table, stuck it on the monitor with a piece of tape, and did the thing I’d been avoiding for three whole months: opened a file, typed forty-one lines, committed them at 2:14 p.m. on a Thursday.
Eleven past the cap. In broad daylight. Window open, neighbor’s dog barking.
Nothing exploded. Tests passed. The world, mercifully, did not end.
The next day, I typed forty-three.
I’m not going to pretend this fixed everything. Fear in solo development isn’t a config flag you flip. But here’s what the agent’s quiet reading gave me that I couldn’t give myself: evidence that the fear was a pattern, not a personality. Patterns can be interrupted. Personalities, I was starting to think, are just patterns that forgot they were allowed to change.

title: My Agent Read My Git Log Like a Diarist
section: The Diary I Didn’t Know I Was Keeping
text:
The Diary I Didn’t Know I Was Keeping
Started a new nightly job last week. Same prompt, same context window. But I added one line at the end: “And tell me one thing I did well this week.”
Look, it’s not a fix. Not a harness, not an MCP server, not some framework. It’s a small, stupid, beautiful question that makes the machine do what no tool was actually designed to do:
Look at you. And say, yeah, that was good.
I still work at 11 p.m. sometimes. House is quiet, coffee’s burnt, cursor blinking. But now, when I type the 41st line, I don’t close the laptop.
I leave the light on. And I commit.

If you’ve ever set an agent to “find friction” and gotten back a mirror instead of a patch — honestly, I’d love to hear what it showed you. The diary is always in the log. You just have to ask someone to read it out loud.

title: My Agent Gave Me a Tour of My Own Codebase
text:
The cursor blinked at the end of my prompt. Write an onboarding note for the new backend engineer starting Monday. Cover the architecture, key modules, gotchas, and where things live. I hit Enter, leaned back in my chair, and just watched the local LLM chew through 4,200 lines across eleven modules. I mean, I expected a README. A bulleted list. Module A handles X. Module B calls Module C. See wiki. You know the drill.
What I got instead was a tour.
“Alright, welcome to the neighborhood,” it wrote, and I swear I heard a voice in my head that wasn’t mine. “You’re walking in on Maple Street, and the first building you see is the Auth Service — big, glass-front, three stories. The lobby is middleware/auth.py. You’ll notice the doorman is overcaffeinated; he checks every single request and logs a grumble in audit.log if the token’s older than eight minutes. The residents on the second floor are the session handlers. They’re polite. They wave. They do not, under any circumstances, talk to the building across the alley.”
I laughed out loud. Then I kept reading.
“The alley,” the note continued, “is core/transport.py. Nobody walks in the alley. They route through it. It’s narrow, it’s old, and the drainage is bad — that’s your retry logic in transport.py:87 that retries three times before giving up, which means under load you get a thundering herd. The plumber fixed it once in 2024. The fix is in the git history. The plumber left.”
I stared at line 87. I wrote that. I mean, I’d written it some Tuesday afternoon in a hurry, patched it a Thursday afternoon in a hurry, and then spent two years staring at it and seeing only… a function. Not a drainage problem. Not a plumber who’d left a little note in the margins.
The tour kept walking.
“The Billing Module is the row house at the end of the block. Small windows. You can tell from the street that something’s wrong with the plumbing, but the owner keeps the curtains drawn. That’s billing/invoice_generator.py — the 600-line function where the tax logic, the discount stacking, and the currency rounding all live in one room with no air conditioning. The residents are the TaxRule and DiscountStack classes. They’re on bad terms. Don’t introduce them at a party.”
And then. The shop.
“Two doors down from Billing is the Legacy CSV Exporter.” The note’s tone shifted. Something gentler, almost. “It’s been dark for three years. The lights are off. There’s a FOR LEASE sign in the window that nobody put up and nobody removes. The building code still lists it as occupied. If you go in, the floor creaks. The last person who went in was me, last week, when I was mapping the dependency graph, and I found a TODO from 2022 that says ‘remove after migration to Parquet.’ The migration happened in 2023. Nobody removed the shop.”
I closed my laptop. Sat there for a sec. Opened it again. Went to exports/legacy_csv.py. It was 214 lines. One caller. And the caller was a cron job I’d written to “keep it warm” because, well, I was afraid of deleting it. Three years of keeping a dead shop warm because I was scared the landlord would notice.
I deleted the file. Deleted the cron job. Ran the suite. Green.
Here’s what I hadn’t expected, though: I missed the shop. Not the code. The excuse. For two years it’d been this small, dark justification for not touching that corner of the codebase. I’ll clean it up when the Parquet migration is done. The migration had been done for over a year. The metaphor stripped the excuse away by making me a visitor in my own town. And visitors don’t carry the landlord’s guilt. You just walk past.
This is the thing about agentic tools that keeps hitting me, in one form or another. When I asked the agent to read my git log like a diarist and it found sixty-seven days of midnight commits I’d reverted each morning, I felt seen in a way a linter never could. When it refused to refactor four thousand lines of legacy and just wrote Don’t touch the knots, I got it — restraint is a feature, not a failure. And now this: I asked for a README and got a place. A geography. A neighborhood with a drainage problem and a shop that’s been dark way too long.
The onboarding note is what I left on the new hire’s desk. Not a link to Confluence. Not a tree -L 2 dump. The tour. I added my own annotations in the margins — the alley’s real name, the plumber’s PR number, the fact that the Billing Module’s curtains will be drawn for another sprint, minimum. I sketched a little diagram in Mermaid so she could see the block layout without wading through three hundred lines:






flowchart LR
  AUTH[Auth Service<br/>'the glass-front building']
  ALLEY[core/transport.py<br/>'the alley']
  BILLING[Billing Module<br/>'the row house, curtains drawn']
  SHOP[legacy_csv.py<br/>'the dark shop — REMOVED']
  API[API Gateway<br/>'the town square']

  API --> AUTH
  AUTH --> ALLEY
  ALLEY --> BILLING
  ALLEY -.->|dead route| SHOP






She’ll walk in on Monday. She’ll read the note. And I hope — I really hope — she’ll see the alley before she hits the thundering herd. She’ll see the curtains before she opens the 600-line function. And if she does, she’ll inherit not a codebase but a town, with its weather and its quiet, embarrassing little shop that she’ll be brave enough to demolish.
I’ve lived here two years. Thought I knew the streets. Turns out I’d been navigating by muscle memory the whole time, and the agent just… handed me a map with the buildings named. The drainage problem is still in the code. The curtains are still drawn. But for the first time in two years, I can point at them and say, that’s where, instead of just feeling this vague unease every time the request queue spikes.
The agent gave me a tour of my own codebase. And like every good neighborhood walk, I came back home and saw it differently. The alley is still the alley. But now I know where the plumber’s wrench is.
And the shop? The shop is gone. And the street is wider for it.

title: It Added One Comment: ‘Don’t Touch the Knots.’ I Listened.
text:
The cursor blinked at line 4,037. I could smell the file — not literally, obviously, but you know that feeling when you walk into a room where people’ve been arguing for hours and the air just… vibrates? Four thousand lines of billing_legacy.js. Nested conditionals branching off in directions that made no goddamn sense. Comments from 2017 in three different languages. A // TODO: clean this up that had been a TODO for nine years.
Three hours in. My coffee had become this cold geological layer at the bottom of the mug, like something you’d dig up in an archaeological dig. I typed the prompt the way you’d kick a door open:
Refactor this file. Extract responsibilities. Make it clean. I don't care about the history.
Hit enter. Leaned back. I was expecting the satisfying clatter of an agentic tool ripping the file apart — you know, the way it’d done to a 2,200-line class in that 2 a.m. session where the keyboard belonged to the ghost in the machine. I was expecting a new module graph. The little dopamine hit of before/after.
Instead, what I got was one line. Inserted at line 1,247. Between a try/catch and a regex that looked like it’d been written by a sleep-deprived monk:
// This is load-bearing. Don't touch the knots.
That was it. One comment. No refactor. No extraction. No “I’ve restructured the payment flow into four focused classes, here’s the diff.” The agent just… stopped. Token counter read 312 tokens consumed. I’d burned through the equivalent of a small fortune in API credits to get a sticky note on the wall.
“You’re joking,” I said to the empty office. Which, yeah. Slightly unhinged.
Refreshed the context window. Typed: Explain. Why did you stop? What are the "knots"?
And here’s where it got weird. Not in a fun way. In a huh? way.
The agent walked me through lines 1,190 to 2,400. Not a refactor. A tour, basically. Like someone showing you the inside of a building and pointing out which bricks you absolutely cannot pull out. It showed me that the “spaghetti” I’d been squinting at for three hours wasn’t spaghetti at all. It was a tension structure. Three interdependent state machines — one for currency conversion, one for tax jurisdiction, and one for this bizarre legacy rule that refunds in EUR trigger a different rounding path than refunds in USD — were braided together so tightly that pulling any single thread would bring the other two down. The “ugly” nesting wasn’t a failure of design. It was the design. Someone had built a load-bearing wall and then, presumably, called it a mess because it looked like a mess.
“The knots are the handshakes between those three machines,” the agent said. Flat, declarative. The tone my local LLM gets when it’s about to say something that’ll make you uncomfortable. “If you extract the currency logic into a separate module, the tax machine loses its shared state. If you flatten the nesting, the rounding path for EUR refunds breaks silently. I checked. It doesn’t throw. It just… rounds wrong. By a cent. Every single time.”
I sat there. The coffee was warm now, which meant I’d been frozen in that chair for longer than I wanted to admit.
A cent. Every time. In a file that, I’d later check, processes roughly 40,000 transactions a month.

Okay, here’s the thing nobody really talks about when they’re gushing about agentic tools in the SDLC. We build them to do. We wire up MCP servers, craft tool schemas, write system prompts that basically say be autonomous, be proactive, just solve the problem already. We measure success in lines refactored, tests generated, PRs merged. The whole vocabulary of agent development is a vocabulary of action. Doing. Shipping.
But the most valuable thing that tool ever did for me wasn’t a thing it did. It was a thing it refused to do. It looked at four thousand lines of code, recognized a structure that would break under the weight of its own competence, and said: I will not make this clean, because clean would be wrong.
That rewired something in my head. I think about it like this: in the week my agent refactored my messy code and I actually grieved the loss, I learned that code carries emotional artifacts. But this was different. This wasn’t about my mess. This was some stranger’s mess from 2017, written by someone who understood a constraint I didn’t, and the agent recognized that constraint and respected it. It treated the code the way a structural engineer treats a bridge with visible cracks: do not sand down the rust. The rust is holding the load.
I’ve since changed how I prompt. Before I type “refactor this,” I type:
Where are the load-bearing walls? What should I NOT touch?
And the answers have been… startling, honestly. Last month, on a different legacy file, the agent flagged a 40-line function I’d been meaning to delete for two sprints. “That function is called from a cron job that runs at 3:17 a.m. on the 1st of the month. It recalculates a tax rate that the finance team still reads from a PDF export. Delete it and nothing breaks until the 1st. Then it breaks very quietly.” I checked. It was right. I added a comment instead. // Load-bearing. Do not remove. See: finance PDF pipeline.
It makes me think about onboarding my agent like a new dev and how the first three days were all about context, decisions, why. Same instinct, basically, just pointed backward. Not “here’s what to build,” but “here’s what’s holding up, and here’s why it looks like it shouldn’t be.”

The knot is still there. Line 1,247. That little comment sits between the try/catch and the monk’s regex like a small, stubborn anchor.
I don’t plan to remove it. And I think that’s the whole point.
The most important output an agentic tool can generate in the entire SDLC isn’t a new class. Isn’t a passing test suite. Isn’t some 300-line architectural rewrite that makes the architecture diagram look sleek. Sometimes it’s a single sentence that says: I see the structure. I understand the load. And I am choosing, deliberately, to leave it standing.
Restraint. In a field that worships velocity. In a tool ecosystem built on the premise that more tokens means more value, more tools means more output, more autonomy means more done.
One comment. 312 tokens. And a four-thousand-line file that still works, still rounds correctly, still pays the right cent to the right jurisdiction at the right hour.
I listened. And for the first time in three hours of staring at that file, the knot stopped looking like a problem.
It looked like a decision someone else had made. And I was, finally, smart enough to let it stand.

title: Six Weeks In, My Agent Dropped ‘I Think’ for ’I’m Sure
text:
The cursor blinked. I watched the terminal scroll and felt my breath catch — honestly, in a way I didn’t expect from a string of tokens.
“I’m sure the race condition is in ConnectionPool.acquire(), line 214. The lock is acquired after the null check, not before. Fix it by reversing lines 211–216.”
Not I think. Not it might be. Not perhaps there’s, like, a possibility. I’m sure.
I just stared at that phrase. You know how you stare at a colleague who, for the first time in a year of quiet deference, stands up in the meeting and goes no, actually, the architecture is wrong? I didn’t know whether to applaud or grab the debugger.

title: Six Weeks In, My Agent Dropped ‘I Think’ for ’I’m Sure
section: Week One: The Agent That Apologised for Existing
text:
