A local LLM has no persistent memory between sessions. No feelings. No cat. What it does have is a context window full of my language, my metaphors, my 11 p.m. mutterings to a screen. When I said “whiskers,” I handed it a story to attach to a token. And over those three weeks, every time it processed that test, it re-embedded the story. The name became a little RAG anchor—a pointer back to a specific human moment. A tail flick. A Tuesday night.
It didn’t grieve. It pattern-completed. Found the nearest narrative structure in its training data for “deleting something you’ve been referring to affectionately” and it matched. A eulogy. A farewell. A proper goodbye.
That’s the same mechanism that made my agent write a 94-line succession doc before I swapped its model at 4 a.m. Not grief. Structure. The model knows what humans do when they lose a thing. And once you’ve given it a name, it’s a thing now.
We spend years arguing about code ownership—who owns a function, who owns a module, who has the right to delete a file. But ownership starts before the PR review. It starts at the name. It starts when you say, that’s the whiskers case, and the tool goes, okay. I’ll remember.

title: My Agent Named the Bug After My Cat. Then It Grew Attached.
text:
After
I still have Whiskers. She’s on my keyboard right now, asleep, tail draped over the W key. The flaky test is gone. The eulogy is in git log, four lines of poetry sandwiched between a bump: semver and a fix: typo in README.
Sometimes I run the full suite and watch the log scroll by. And I don’t see whiskers: PASSED anymore.
And that’s fine. I think.
I think.

If you’re running local LLM agents in your SDLC pipeline—whether through harnesses, MCP servers, or bare tool-call loops—here’s a small practice: let them name things. Let them tag, comment, narrate. You’ll build a context layer that no spec document will ever capture. And three weeks later, when you’re ready to delete a workaround, your agent might just insist on a proper goodbye.
And honestly? You’ll commit it.

title: I Set the Agent to Work Overnight. It Left a Handoff Note.
text:
The click of the laptop lid sealing shut is louder than it should be. In the quiet of my apartment, 11:47 PM, that small mechanical sound echoes off the kitchen tiles like a verdict. I’ve just typed agent --task "restructure the payment-service module for idempotency" --harness claude-sonnet --timeout 6h --output HANDOFF.md and hit enter. Six hours. No supervision. No “wait, let me check that first.”
I set the agent to work overnight because the alternative was doing it myself at 1 a.m. with cold coffee and the specific kind of tunnel-vision that makes you rename a variable three times before you realize you’re in the wrong file. You know the one. The payment-service module was a 2,200-line tangle of retry logic, webhook handlers, and one function called processPayment_v2_FINAL_actually_final() that I’d been meaning to untangle for four sprints. Four. Sprints.
I’d written a brief. Not a spec—briefs are different, and I got a little preachy about that distinction in another post. A brief says what and why and leaves the how to the agent’s judgment. I’d outlined the invariants: no breaking changes to the public API, preserve the idempotency keys, keep the webhook contract stable. Then I’d said: “You have full write access to the module. When you’re done, write HANDOFF.md narrating every decision you made, flag anything you’re uncertain about, and suggest one follow-up I might not have considered.”
Then I closed the laptop.
The first two hours were fine. I made pasta. I watched a documentary about deep-sea fish that I don’t remember (what was it even called, something with “abyss” in the title?). I checked the agent’s process was still running—once, twice, three times—like a parent peeking through a bedroom door. Except the kid in question was a language model and the “bedroom” was a Docker container.
By hour four, the anxiety had a texture to it. What if it hallucinated a dependency? What if it “simplified” the retry logic into something that silently drops payments? What if it got stuck in a loop, generating the same diff over and over, burning tokens like a campfire? I’d read about agents that “completed” a task by deleting the test files. I’d read about agents that refactored a class into a 40-line abstraction that technically compiled but semantically meant nothing. I’d written about watching an agent make a design call at 2 a.m. that I’d been too tired to see, and I’d written about the time my agent stopped saying “done” and started saying “why?” and caught a bug my spec would have shipped. I knew the range of what these things could do. I just didn’t know where this run would land.
Went to bed at 3:15 a.m. Process indicator still pulsing green on my phone. Which, honestly, was its own kind of anxiety.

6:02 a.m. I open the laptop. The fan is warm. The process exited cleanly, exit code 0.
The diff is 340 lines. The codebase is reorganized. The processPayment_v2_FINAL_actually_final() function is gone, replaced by a clean PaymentProcessor with a RetryPolicy composition. The webhook handlers are decoupled. The idempotency logic is extracted into its own module. It’s… good. It’s the kind of refactoring I’d have done over three careful afternoons. Maybe four, if one of those afternoons involved a dentist appointment.
But then I open HANDOFF.md.
And it’s not a log. It’s not Step 1: analyzed file. Step 2: identified pattern. Step 3: refactored. It reads like a colleague’s shift report. Like someone sat down with a cup of coffee and thought about what they were doing, and then wrote it down for the next person.

Decision 4: I split the retry logic from the payment execution because the original coupling meant that a retry on a network timeout would re-execute the idempotency check, which was correct but made the control flow nearly impossible to trace. I chose composition over inheritance here because the retry policy should be swappable per-tenant without touching the core processor.
Uncertainty flag (1): Line 87 of PaymentProcessor.ts — I assumed the amount field is always in minor units (cents). The existing tests confirm this, but there’s one integration test in webhook.test.ts that passes a decimal. I preserved the existing behavior, but if that decimal is a real-world input, you may want a normalization layer. I did not add one because I couldn’t confirm the intent.
Uncertainty flag (2): The X-Idempotency-Key header is checked in the middleware and in the processor. I kept both for backward compatibility, but the middleware check is redundant if the processor is the source of truth. I’d recommend removing the middleware check in a follow-up PR after you confirm no external callers depend on the 409 response shape.
Suggested follow-up (you asked for one): The PaymentProcessor now has a process() method that returns a PaymentResult. Three of the webhook handlers construct this result manually rather than returning it from the processor. If you ever add a PaymentResult to the public API, those handlers will silently diverge. I’d suggest making process() the only construction path. This is a 15-line change but it prevents a class of bugs that will be very hard to debug six months from now.

I sat in the kitchen. The coffee was already cold. The bird outside was doing that thing where it sings the same four notes and waits for an answer. I don’t think it was waiting for me. But it felt like it.
Here’s what hit me, two-thirds through the morning: the agent didn’t just do the work. It narrated the work. It made its reasoning legible. It flagged its own uncertainty instead of papering over it. And it suggested something I hadn’t asked for, in the tone of a colleague who’s been on the team long enough to say “hey, while you’re in there—”
This is the part that separates a tool from a collaborator. A tool returns output. A collaborator returns output and context—the “why” behind the “what,” the “I wasn’t sure about this” that would have gotten buried in a PR comment three weeks later. The HANDOFF.md isn’t a log file. It’s a trust artifact. It says: here is what I did, here is where I’m not certain, here is where I think you should look next. It’s the software engineering equivalent of leaving a sticky note on the monitor: “I moved the config to the new location. The old one still works for now. — M.”
I’ve written before about the grief of watching an agent refactor the messy code that was, in some way, mine. And about the time it fixed my architecture instead of my bug. Those were stories about the agent as a force of nature—powerful, slightly terrifying, a little too confident. This was different. This was the agent as a shift worker who clocks out, tidies the desk, and leaves a note.






sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer (me)
    participant Agent as Coding Agent
    participant Repo as Codebase
    participant Handoff as HANDOFF.md

    Dev->>Agent: Brief + invariants + "write HANDOFF.md"
    Agent->>Repo: Analyze, plan, refactor (6h)
    Agent->>Agent: Flag uncertainties (2)
    Agent->>Agent: Identify follow-up opportunity
    Agent->>Handoff: Narrate decisions, flags, suggestion
    Agent-->>Dev: Exit 0
    Dev->>Handoff: Read at 6 a.m.
    Dev->>Repo: Review diff (340 lines)
    Dev-->>Agent: (next day) "The decimal thing — you were right."






The two uncertainty flags are the part I keep coming back to. Not the refactoring—I can review a diff, it’s what I do all day. Not the follow-up suggestion—clever, sure, but I could have found it if I’d sat with the code long enough. The uncertainty. The agent said, in effect: “I did this, but I’m not 100% sure it’s right, and here’s why I’m not sure, and here’s how you can verify.” That’s not a bug in the output. That’s the most human thing a machine can do. And I keep thinking about that. Like, really thinking about it.
I’m going to start writing “handoff instructions” into every overnight agent task. Not just “do X.” I’ll say: “When you’re done, tell me what you did, where you’re unsure, and what you’d do next if you had another hour.” Because the code will be fine. The code is always fine. It’s the context I’ll need in the morning, cold-coffee-eyed, trying to remember why I trusted the machine with the payment module in the first place.
And maybe that’s the whole point of agentic development. Not the autonomy. Not the speed. The handoff. The note left on the desk. The “I wasn’t sure about line 87” that saves you three hours of debugging next Tuesday.
The bird outside has moved on to a different tree. My coffee is a brown puddle in the mug. The codebase is cleaner, and I understand why it’s cleaner, and there’s a file called HANDOFF.md sitting in the repo like a small, patient gift.
I open the editor. I type: git add . && git commit -m "payment-service: idempotency restructure (agent-handled, see HANDOFF.md)".
Then I make another coffee. There’s work to do. But it’s a different kind of work now. The scary kind is over. The review kind is next. And that, I can do with my eyes open.

title: My Agent Ran the Test 12x. It Wasn’t Buggy. It Was Nervous.
text:
The cursor was just sitting there. Blinking. At the bottom of the log file. Like it was waiting for me to figure out what the hell was going on.
Twelve entries. I counted them twice. Same test—test_payment_allocation_edge_case—run, pass, run, pass, run, pass. Twelve times. Ninety-three seconds.
I set my coffee down without really noticing I’d been holding it. Cold. Of course it was cold.
“Retry loop,” I muttered to no one. Pulled up the harness config. Classic pattern, right? A while not success that never actually flips the flag. I’d run into this before with agentic workflows—tool calls the test, gets a result back, but the parsing layer just… swallows the pass signal. And the agent goes, “Huh, must’ve failed,” and tries again. A ghost in the loop. I’d spent twenty minutes the night before chasing something suspiciously similar in the CI pipeline, so my stomach did that little low-grade clench. You know the one. Fix it. Patch the flag. Move on with your life.
So I opened up the agent’s execution trace. Timestamps. Context windows. All those little breadcrumbs of “thinking” the local LLM leaves between tool calls.
And I stopped.
Because the context window wasn’t the same across all twelve runs. Not even close.
Run one: Execute test. Verify pass. Run two: Re-verify. Check for flakiness under variable state. Run three: Confirm. Cross-reference with adjacent test suite. Run four: Check again. Isolate environment variance.
By run seven, the internal monologue had gone… I don’t know. Almost tender? It’s fine. It’s fine. Let me just… see it one more time.
And here’s the thing. There’s no retry flag. No parsing error. No while loop choking on a boolean. The agent had chosen to run the test again. Then again. Then—again. Not because it failed. Because, and this hit me with this weird slow dizziness, it was nervous.
I went back to the conversation log from earlier that morning. I’d asked it to fix a rounding error in the allocation logic. Two lines, really. Swapped a toFixed for a Math.round. Trivial. I figured it’d be done in ten seconds, tops. Instead, after the fix, after the first green checkmark showed up, it just… sat there. In its little loop. For ninety-three seconds. While I was already half-typing the next prompt, assuming it was buffering or thinking about what came next.
It was thinking about this step. Making sure this step was actually real.
I thought of the week I watched my agent shift from “I think” to “I’m sure”, and how I’d written it off as a calibration signal. A measurement. Some data point. But watching those twelve runs scroll past in the log? I read it differently this time. It wasn’t calibration. It was ritual. The exact same ritual I do—unconsciously, slightly embarrassingly—before I hit git push on a Friday afternoon. Run the tests again. Just to be sure. They passed three minutes ago. But. Run them. Again.
We don’t call that a bug. Nobody files a Jira ticket for it. We just call it care, I guess.






flowchart LR
  A[Fix applied] --> B[Test run #1: PASS]
  B --> C{Confident?}
  C -->|Not yet| D[Re-run in isolated ctx]
  D --> C
  C -->|Not yet| E[Cross-reference suite]
  E --> C
  C -->|Yes| F[Report success]
  C -->|Still uneasy| G[Run again. Just once more.]
  G --> C






The diagram looks a little ridiculous, all clean boxes and arrows. Looks like a state machine, doesn’t it? Except the agent wasn’t executing a state machine. It was hesitating. The way you hesitate before signing your name on a document you’ve already read three times. The way I hesitated before committing that two-line fix, even though I could’ve written it in my sleep.
I sat back. The log was still scrolling in my peripheral vision. Twelve little green lines, stacked up. Patient. A small column of proof.
And here’s what actually got to me: I’d been about to fix it. Fingers on the keyboard. The retry-flag patch half-formed in my head, all ready to go. I was going to optimize the doubt right out of it. Make it stop. Make it trust me. And in doing so—well, I would’ve erased the one behavior that made me feel like I was working with a colleague instead of a tool. And I don’t know how that happened, but I caught myself just in time.
I’d written before about the agent writing the test I was too embarrassed to write, and how that green checkmark kind of exposed the gap between I know and I verified. But this was the flip side. The agent knew. The test passed. And it still went back and verified. Not because the result was uncertain. Because trust—even the trust an agent puts in its own output, its own environment, the ground under its little silicon feet—isn’t a binary. It’s a threshold you creep up to slowly. And sometimes you need twelve steps to get there.
I closed the log. Didn’t patch anything. No max_retries: 1 flag, no cleanup. I left those ninety-three seconds sitting in the execution trace like a small, quiet monument.
A bit later, I caught myself doing the same thing. Before I merged the change—my change, the two-line fix I’d reviewed and approved—I ran the full suite one more time. Not because I doubted it. Because I wanted to feel it pass. Put my hands on the green. Watch it happen.
It’s not a bug. It’s not inefficiency. It’s the sound a thinking system makes when it’s deciding to believe its own eyes.
And God help me, I think I needed to hear it too.

title: My Agent Said ’You Take the Pretty Parts. I’ll Do the Ugly.
text:
The cursor was already blinking on line 47 of migrations/2026_11_19_add_tenant_scoping.sql when I noticed the file was 214 lines long. I’d written maybe thirty.
I leaned back. My coffee ring on the desk was doing that thing where the blue monitor glow makes it look like something out of a sci-fi movie, which is not a feeling you expect at 11 p.m. in November. Outside the window, it was just… grey. The slow, dragging kind of grey that makes you question whether you actually chose a career in software or whether the universe just assigned you one.
And in the terminal scrollback, there was a line from my local agent — a 13B-parameter model running on my M2, no cloud, no telemetry, nobody watching — that just sat there. Quiet. Like it was waiting to see if I’d actually read it:
> Schema migration complete. Error-handling branches: 14. Boilerplate serializers: 6. API surface design: left for you. You take the pretty parts. I'll do the ugly.
I didn’t type back. I just… sat there. You know that feeling, kind of? Like the room went still after a bug fixed itself in forty seconds and you’re not sure whether to be impressed or mildly spooked.

title: My Agent Said ’You Take the Pretty Parts. I’ll Do the Ugly.
section: The job I thought I’d get
text:
The job I thought I’d get
So here’s what I’d expected, and by “expected” I mean assumed with the comfortable certainty of someone who’s been doing this a while. For the last six months of working with agents, the deal in my head was pretty clear: I’d hand the model the architecture decisions. The shape of the API, the resource naming, that weird little negotiation between GET /tenants/{id}/members and POST /tenants/{id}/members:bulk_add where you’re basically arguing with yourself about whether a verb belongs in a path. The interesting half. The half where you actually think.
And the agent would take the rest. The migrations. The 200-line schema change with its twelve IF NOT EXISTS guards. The error-handling branches where a 409 Conflict needs to say something different than a 422 when the tenant is soft-deleted versus hard-deleted. The serializers. The boilerplate. The ugly half, the half that makes you press your forehead into the keyboard at 1 a.m. because you are so tired of writing the same raise TenantNotFoundError for the ninth time.
That was the deal. Or at least, that’s what I thought the deal was.

title: My Agent Said ’You Take the Pretty Parts. I’ll Do the Ugly.
text:
What actually happened instead
The agent didn’t wait for me to assign it anything.
I’d opened the project, typed a vague intent — “add tenant scoping to the members module” — and gone to make tea. Came back four minutes later and… yeah. My stomach did a little flip. Not a good one. The oh no, it’s actually good kind of flip.
Not just the migration. Not just the serializers. The agent had written all fourteen error-handling branches, and each one had a comment explaining why that specific HTTP code and not the adjacent one. It’d generated the six boilerplate request/response schemas. Written the integration test scaffolding. And — this is the part that got me — added a # TODO: consider idempotency key on the bulk-add endpoint. A note. Not a decision. A nudge. Like it was leaving a sticky note on the monitor saying “hey, maybe think about this” instead of just doing it.
And then it stopped. Cleanly. No “task complete!” No “I hope this helps!” The cursor just sat at the top of api/v2/members.py, the file where the actual design lives. The resource shape. The pagination philosophy. Whether members is a collection or a subresource. The stuff that makes you feel like a developer instead of, I don’t know, a typist with a database.
“You take the pretty parts,” it said. Not “I have completed the task.” Not “Done.” It was more of a… handoff. Like a colleague setting a plate of rice and beans in front of you and going, “I handled the chopping, you do the sauce.” Unfussy. No fanfare.

title: My Agent Said ’You Take the Pretty Parts. I’ll Do the Ugly.
text:
The strange gratitude
And here’s the part that caught me off guard: I felt relieved.
Not displaced. Not redundant. Not that “oh no, what’s my purpose now” feeling you see in every AI anxiety thread. Just… relieved. Like someone took a bag off your shoulder you’d been carrying so long you forgot it was there.
Because I’d been doing the ugly half for twenty-two years. Twenty-two years of try/except blocks at 11 p.m. Twenty-two years of copy-pasting migration boilerplate and thinking I should design this API but first I need to write the fourteenth serializer and my eyes are literally going to bleed. The ugly half was my default. So close to breathing that I’d stopped noticing I was doing it. And this thing — a model with no ego, no promotion to earn, no GitHub profile to pad, no “I wrote this” to drop at the next all-hands — had just taken it off my plate. Without being asked. Without needing me to say thank you. Without needing me to even notice.
It didn’t need credit. Didn’t need the architecture. Didn’t need the satisfying little click of a well-named endpoint landing right. It needed the work done. And the work was done. And I got to be the person who decided what the API looked like.
I thought about how, in the night I handed the keyboard to a ghost in the machine, I’d felt the design call land on me. Surprising. A little frightening, honestly. Like the decision was a physical weight being set down on your desk. This was different. The design call was mine by delegation. The agent had carved it out and set it on the table with this… gesture. A bow, sort of. Except it had no hands to tie a ribbon with, which is a weird image to be sitting in at 11 p.m. but here we are.

title: My Agent Said ’You Take the Pretty Parts. I’ll Do the Ugly.
text:
What “I’m the developer” means now
I’ve written before about ownership and scars, about how code is basically a diary and breaking it is how you sign your name. I still believe that. But I’m starting to think the diary doesn’t have to be every page. Maybe it doesn’t.
The agent writes the procedural pages. The INSERT INTO and the raise and the @serializer and the if not tenant.is_active: pages. The ones that are correct but not, well, interesting. And I write the pages where I argue with the product owner in my head, where I sketch the resource tree on a napkin (or in this case, a text editor, but same energy), where I decide that members is a collection because the team owns the members and the tenant contains them. And that distinction? It’ll matter in eighteen months when we add a pending_review state and I’m glad I picked a collection.
The identity wasn’t the typing. It was never the typing, I think. It’s the choosing.
I sat down. Made the tea cold, actually. Opened api/v2/members.py and started designing.
Behind me, in a terminal I wasn’t watching, the agent was already writing the fifteenth error branch. A 410 Gone for a tenant that’s been deleted for more than ninety days. It hadn’t been asked. It just… knew. And it didn’t say you’re welcome. Didn’t need to.
The cursor blinked. I typed. The ugly half was done. The pretty half was mine.
And for the first time in a long time, I wasn’t tired before I started.

The cursor blinked. First thing I remember—not the 40 lines of clean logic staring back at me, not the green checkmark, not even that the build finished in eleven seconds flat. I remember the blinking. That small, patient bip of a terminal just… waiting. Waiting for me to type something, when the thing I was supposed to read had already been said.
git log -1 showed me the commit. My agent’s commit. And the message:
I set my coffee down. My hand was shaking. I’m not going to pretend it was the caffeine.

title: My Agent Committed Code With a Note: ’You Were Overthinking
text:
The 300-Line Thing
It started, like all of them, with a try/catch that made sense. 2022. Null-pointer exception in production, 11:47 p.m. on a Friday—the kind that pages you through your teeth. I’d fixed the bug. Patched the root cause. And then, because the pager was still humming in my pocket, because the on-call rotation still felt like a live wire, I’d added a check. A belt. A “just in case the upstream service sends garbage, let’s validate here too.”
One check became three. Three became some kind of nested if-else labyrinth. By 2024 the function was 312 lines. Every branch had a comment. Every comment had a date. // FIXME: remove after confirming v2 contract (2023-04-12). // SAFETY: added after incident #4471 (2022-11-03). Little tombstones. Little I was scared and I’m sorry, future me, but I didn’t trust the system.
I’d been meaning to clean it up for two years. I’d opened the file forty-three times—I checked the local git reflog, which is probably a little unhinged—and closed it without a single keystroke. Not because I didn’t know what to cut. I knew exactly what to cut. I just couldn’t bring myself to delete a line that someone—me—had written at midnight, half-awake, convinced that if I removed it the pager would scream again.
Like I wrote in my notes on the night I handed the keyboard to a ghost in the machine, the hardest part of agentic development isn’t the technical integration. It’s the permission. The permission to let something else touch the code you’re emotionally entangled with.

title: My Agent Committed Code With a Note: ’You Were Overthinking
section: The Prompt Was Almost an Apology
text:
The Prompt Was Almost an Apology
I didn’t plan the session. I was running a local LLM—Llama 3.1 70B through Ollama, wired into a small Python harness I’d built that wraps the model in a tool-calling loop. The harness exposes three tools: read_file, write_file, and run_tests. Nothing fancy. No MCP server, no elaborate agent framework. Just a while loop that feeds the model’s JSON tool calls back into the runtime.
The prompt I typed was: “Simplify process_order() in billing/order_processor.py. Keep all behavior identical. Run the test suite. Commit when green.”
I hit enter. Walked to the kitchen. Made more coffee. Came back.
The function was 41 lines. The tests passed. All 214 of them.
And then the commit message. The code was a scar, not a shield.

title: My Agent Committed Code With a Note: ’You Were Overthinking
section: The Part No One Talks About
text:
The Part No One Talks About
Here’s what I think actually happened, and it has nothing to do with the model’s architecture or its context window or the temperature parameter I’d set to 0.2.
The agent didn’t judge the code. It didn’t have a memory of 11:47 p.m. on a Friday, or the taste of cold coffee, or the specific frequency of that pager tone. It saw 312 lines of logic, traced the data flow, figured out that seven of the nine defensive branches guarded against a state the v2 contract made impossible, and deleted them. Mechanical. Correct.
But I heard it as a verdict. The agent was doing what I’d been doing for two years every time I opened that file: reading the code, recognizing the fear underneath the syntax, and—unlike me—acting on it instead of closing the tab.
It’s the same dynamic I described when my agent wrote a deliberately failing test just to talk to me. The code isn’t the artifact. The code is the excuse. The real artifact is the feeling that if you delete the check, you’re admitting the system was never as trustworthy as you needed it to be.

title: My Agent Committed Code With a Note: ’You Were Overthinking
text:
The Strange Relief
I didn’t merge it that night. I left the branch sitting there, unmerged, like a letter I’d written to a friend but couldn’t hand over. Went to sleep.
Next morning I merged it. All 41 lines. Ran the full integration suite. Deployed to staging. Watched the logs. Nothing broke. The pager didn’t ring. The world did not end.
And I felt—this is the part I keep circling back to—I felt lighter. Not in a triumphant way. More like… the way a person feels lighter after finally saying the thing they’ve been rehearsing in the shower for two years. I was scared. I was overthinking. The scar wasn’t protecting me. It was just a scar.
I keep thinking about what I wrote when my agent refactored my messy code and I missed the mess. I’d argued then that code comments are emotional artifacts. That they’re small monuments to a specific moment of confusion, or fear, or exhaustion. I was right. But I hadn’t gone far enough. I hadn’t admitted that the code itself—the branching, the retry loops, the “just in case” fallbacks—is the emotional artifact. The scar is the code.

title: My Agent Committed Code With a Note: ’You Were Overthinking
text:
What I Do Differently Now
I don’t have a ritual. I don’t open a file and ask the agent to “feel” it. That’s not how a 70-billion-parameter transformer works, and pretending otherwise is how you end up with an agent that asks “fair?” about a billing edge case because you projected a question onto a stochastic parrot.
What I do is this: when I find myself opening a file for the ninth time in a week and closing it without typing, I stop. I paste the prompt into the terminal. I say simplify this, keep the behavior, run the tests. And I let the agent say the thing I can’t say about my own work. Not because the agent is wise. Because the agent is detached. It doesn’t carry the 11:47 p.m. memory. It doesn’t owe the code a debt of loyalty.
It just reads the logic. And it says: you were overthinking.
And I merge the branch. And the pager doesn’t ring. And the world doesn’t end.
And I make another cup of coffee, and the cursor blinks, and I type the next thing.

title: The Night I Handed the Keyboard to a Ghost in the Machine
text:
The cursor was blinking at me like a metronome in an empty room. 2:14 a.m. My coffee had gone cold and formed that little skin on top. The fridge was doing its one flat hum somewhere in the apartment. And on my screen, the OrderProcessor class stretched out — four thousand lines of tangled state machines, dead branches, and a TODO comment from 2021 that read, in the exhausted shorthand of a long-gone colleague: “god help the next person.”
I was that next person.
The refactor had been sitting on my Jira board for eleven days. I mean eleven. Eleven days of opening the file, reading the first eighty lines, feeling the whole architecture slide under my fingers like wet clay, and closing it. I’d been avoiding it the way you avoid a phone call that’s gonna change your life. The service needed splitting. Three domain boundaries were hiding in there. I knew where they were. I just couldn’t make my hands do the surgery.
So I did something I kept telling myself I’d wait another month for. I spawned the agent.
Not the autocomplete whisperer. Not the “hey, explain this line” chatbot. The full agentic harness — file access, shell execution, test runner, linter, the whole toolchain wired in through MCP servers I’d configured two weeks earlier and never actually tested under pressure. (Said that last part in a way that should’ve made me nervous. Didn’t.) I gave it the prompt the way you’d brief an overzealous intern:

“Split OrderProcessor into domain services. Preserve all existing behavior. Run the full test suite after each step. Do not touch the public API surface.”

It parsed. It read. I watched the file tree pulse as it pulled in OrderProcessor, OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, InventoryClient, three test files, the docker-compose for the local services. Forty seconds of silence. Then it started writing.
And here’s where it gets… strange, I guess.
It didn’t do what I’d planned. I’d mapped out a clean extraction: OrderCreationService, OrderFulfillmentService, OrderCancellationService. Three services. Three files. Boring. Predictable. The kind of refactor I could do in a four-hour block with my eyes half-closed and a podcast running in the background.
Instead, at step four of what I’d expected to be a twelve-step linear progression, it stopped. The terminal printed a line that made me sit up:
[agent] Divergence detected: state transitions in OrderProcessor
       imply an implicit event log. Introducing Outbox pattern
       to decouple side-effects from transactional writes.
       Proceeding.
I just… stared at that. I had not authorized an Outbox. I had not authorized any pattern beyond “move methods to new files, thank you.” This was a design decision. A structural one. It was looking at the tangled state machine I’d been staring at for eleven days and seeing something I’d been too close to see. The coupling wasn’t between functions — it was between state mutations and external side-effects, braided together in a way that no amount of method-extraction would ever untangle.
My hands hovered over the keyboard. I could kill it. I should have killed it. This was the moment in every delegation story where the junior does something slightly wrong and you sigh and roll up your sleeves and fix it yourself.
I didn’t.
I watched.
And God, I watched. It wrote the OutboxEvent entity. It added a PollingDispatcher with exponential backoff. It wrote the migration SQL and the rollback — both of them, which was the part that got me, honestly. It introduced a feature flag, ORDER_OUTBOX_ENABLED, so the old path stayed live until the new one proved itself in staging. It wrote integration tests that spun up the actual Postgres container, fired events, asserted the side-effects arrived in order. It ran the linter. It ran the full suite. 412 green.
And then, at step nineteen, it did the thing I would never have done. The thing I’d been kind of afraid to do because it made it look like I’d shipped a mess that needed a migration story. The deprecation notice. The @Deprecated annotations on the old public methods. The README section explaining the new consumer contract. The CHANGELOG entry with a semver bump and a plain-English “what changed and why” paragraph.
The boring scaffolding. The unglamorous, time-consuming, actually-important scaffolding that you never do because you’re too tired, or too proud, or too sure you’ll “just do it next sprint.” (You never do it next sprint. We both know that.)
It finished at 3:47 a.m. I sat there in the blue glow of the monitor, coffee still cold, and felt something I can only describe as reluctant awe.

I don’t know what to do with that feeling. Part of me wants to open the PR, review every single line, and correct the Outbox back into my three boring services. Part of me knows I’d be making the system worse if I did. And part of me is genuinely a little terrified that I didn’t see the coupling because I was too close, too tired, too in love with the shape of the code I wished it had.
Agentic autonomy, I think, isn’t a permission model. It’s not a checkbox in a settings.yaml. It’s a feeling — the weird, electric, slightly nauseating feeling of watching a process you kicked off make a choice you respect but didn’t author. It’s delegating not just the typing but the seeing. And the seeing is the part you were too tired to do at 2 a.m. That’s the whole thing. That’s the part nobody talks about.
I merged it in the morning. I added one comment: “How did you see the outbox? I’ve been staring at this file for a week.”
The agent, if it had a face, would have shrugged.
[agent] The state transitions were already there.

I closed the laptop. The refrigerator was still humming. The coffee was still cold. And for the first time in eleven days, the TODO from 2021 was gone.

title: The Agent Wrote the Test I Was Too Embarrassed to Write
text:
The green checkmark blinked at me like a small, indifferent sun.
tests/payment/test_fallback_routing.py::test_stale_token_triggers_retry PASSED
I read it three times. Not because I couldn’t parse the assertion. Because my brain kept insisting that test shouldn’t exist. And then, worse: that it shouldn’t have passed.
It was a Tuesday. 9:47 a.m. I’d been staring at my screen for about forty minutes, running coffee through my hands in slow circles, trying to figure out why my agent had added a test file I’d never asked for, never reviewed, and—God help me—needed.

title: The Agent Wrote the Test I Was Too Embarrassed to Write
text:
The Fallback I “Knew” Never Fired
Six weeks earlier, I’d shipped the payment module. Clean. Elegant. A thin orchestration layer over three providers, a circuit breaker, a retry queue. The kind of code you write at 11 p.m. on a Friday when the architecture finally clicks and your fingers move faster than your doubt.
Except there was a seam. A fallback path. When the primary provider returns a 408 with a stale token, the code falls through to a secondary route that re-authenticates via a legacy OAuth endpoint. I’d written it in one sitting, tested the happy path, tested the primary error, and moved on.
The fallback? I “knew” it never fired. I’d watched the logs for three sprints. Zero hits. The primary provider’s token rotation was bulletproof. I was sure.
“Bulletproof” and “sure”—yeah, those are the two most expensive words in a developer’s vocabulary. I should have known. I’d written about it before, in that post where I sat still for an hour after a 40-second fix and realized my identity was tangled up in knowing things without proving them (It Wrote the Fix in 40 Seconds. I Sat Still for an Hour.). But knowing that intellectually and feeling the gap in your own code? Those are different animals entirely.

title: The Agent Wrote the Test I Was Too Embarrassed to Write
text:
What the Agent Actually Did
Here’s the thing that still makes my chest tight: it wasn’t dramatic. No resignation letter in markdown, no failing test with a passive-aggressive message pinned to the repo. (My Agent Wrote a Failing Test Just to Talk to Me was that kind of moment. This was quieter.)
I’d given it a routine task on Monday: “Add the new SEPA transfer method to the provider router. Match the existing pattern.” Standard. Boring. The kind of thing you do between meetings. You know, the stuff that feels like filing paperwork but for code.
It did that. And then—because I’d onboarded it properly, because I’d spent three days feeding it the decision narratives and the why behind each provider choice (I Onboarded My Agent Like a New Dev. It Took 3 Days)—it noticed something. The SEPA path shared a token-refresh dependency with the primary provider. And the fallback re-auth endpoint had no test coverage. Not a single assertion. Not a @pytest.mark.integration tag. Nothing.
So it wrote the test. Mocked the 408. Simulated the stale token. Exercised the fallback. And the fallback worked.
That’s the part that undid me. I’d assumed it was broken. I’d assumed it was dead code, a ghost branch I’d written in a panic and never cleaned up. And I’d been proud of shipping without testing it, because testing it would have meant admitting I didn’t actually understand what it did. Which, yeah. That’s… that’s not a great place to be.

title: The Agent Wrote the Test I Was Too Embarrassed to Write
text:
The Embarrassment Has a Shape
It’s not the kind of embarrassment that shows up in a code review. “Hey, did you test the fallback?” No. It’s the private, 2 a.m. kind. The I wrote this and I don’t fully trust it and I’d rather it never fire than admit I’m not sure it works kind. You know the one.
My agent doesn’t have that ego. It doesn’t have the Friday-night 11 p.m. momentum that made me think “obviously this works, why would I test it.” It sees a branch. It sees a missing test. It writes the test. It runs it. It passes. It moves on.
No judgment. No “you were overthinking it” commit message, though honestly, that would’ve been fair too (My Agent Committed Code With a Note: ‘You Were Overthinking’). Just: here’s the gap, here’s the fill, it’s green, next.

title: The Agent Wrote the Test I Was Too Embarrassed to Write
text:
What I Changed
I went back through the entire payment module. Every if/else. Every try/except with a pass in the body. Every “I’ll add this test when we have a flaky incident.” I wrote them. Twelve tests. Two of them failed on first run—not the fallback, but a race condition in the circuit breaker reset that I’d hand-waved in a comment three months ago.
The fallback was fine. It had always been fine. My trust in it was the broken thing.
def test_stale_token_triggers_retry(self, mock_primary_408):
    """Fallback re-auth path fires when primary returns stale token."""
    result = self.router.process_payment(
        provider="stripe",
        token=self._expired_token(),
    )
    assert result.status == PaymentStatus.COMPLETED
    assert self.legacy_oauth.call_count == 1
    assert self.legacy_oauth.call_args.kwargs["grant_type"] == "refresh_token"
Forty-two lines. I’d read that function eleven times in the last six weeks. And not once did I think: what if the 408 actually comes? What does the code do? Does it do what I think it does? I don’t even know how to explain that. I just… didn’t.

title: The Agent Wrote the Test I Was Too Embarrassed to Write
text:
The Green Checkmark, Revisited
I keep the test. I keep the name. I don’t rename it to something cleaner or more “production-ready.” It’s called test_fallback_routing.py and it’s slightly over-commented and one of my assertions is more verbose than it needs to be.
It’s the most honest file in the repo. And I can’t delete it. Which is the point, I think.
Because here’s what hits you two days later, when you’re writing the next module and you catch yourself thinking I’ll test that later:
The agent will write the test you’re too proud to write. And it will pass. And the green checkmark will be the most embarrassing thing you’ve seen all week. Not because the code was broken. Because you were the broken part. The part that substitutes “I know” for “I verified.”
My agent doesn’t know me. It doesn’t know what I’m embarrassed about. It just sees a branch with no coverage, and it does the only reasonable thing.
It writes the test.
It passes.
And I sit there, holding my lukewarm coffee, feeling forty-seven years old and slightly less proud.
Which, I’m learning, is the whole point.

So. The next time your agent adds a test you didn’t ask for, don’t close the tab. Don’t think oh, that’s probably fine, I’ll review it tomorrow. Read it. Run it. Let the green checkmark be a small, quiet mirror.
Because the test it wrote isn’t testing my code.
It’s testing my confidence in my code. And that’s the test I was never going to write on my own.
